subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO REDUCE INTEREST RATES- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an urgent and important matter.
Considering that the Pepin Board has not seen fit to control interest rates, particularly debit and credit rates, considering that the gap now exceeds 4 per cent, which is the largest in recent years, and considering also that current interest rates are really very high, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the explanation is quite simple: there is no reason whatsoever to jeopardize the hopes of all those taking part in the physically disabled Olympiad, except for the South African team. speechtext:
Why is this session being continued? Is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) trying to establish a record to compete with the despicable record of the long parliament in the reign of Charles I? Is it because this government hates parliament? I underline that. I have sat here under several prime ministers who, while we disagreed on the facts in respect of many matters of legislation, agreed-until the present administration-that parliament is supreme.

I laughed when I read of the visitation in Cuba when the Prime Minister cuddled up to Castro. Having regard to the way in which parliament is being treated and controlled, I can only say that the Prime Minister of Canada would certainly be able to give some lessons to Castro, provided that gentleman ever set up a democratic government. We go on and on. Why is there the delay? It is simply because the government does not know what it is doing and does not have the legislation ready.
That brings me to the matter of the control of parliament. Today we had evidence of the endeavour to intimidate members of parliament. When members of the opposition ask a question which implies anything to which the government objects, the Prime Minister-as he did today-rises and says, "State a charge". The Prime Minister adds words to this effect, "Does the hon. member believe in what he has said, for unless he can establish it, his seat is in jeopardy." In other words, if one says anything critical of this government, then that is wrongdoing and in that case the member must resign.
Mr. Speaker, that is the greatest nonsense I have ever heard. It has no basis in the Parliament of Canada or in the Parliament of Great Britain, the mother of parliaments. It is merely an endeavour to intimidate by threat. If I say anything in the nature of a threat, I would be glad to be number one to come under the bat of the Prime Minister. Going on from there, the Prime Minister says that if anyone makes a statement in the nature of a charge, he must prove it. All I have to say about that is that naturally the matter would be submitted to a committee of the House with a majority of Liberal members. I would like to know what the result would be. I do not want to predict. Even with the integrity, knowledge and wisdom of Liberal members, I doubt whether they would vote exculpation, regardless of the evidence.
Before I went into the question of this childish, transparent endeavour to intimidate, I called the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He has sat in parliament for many, many years. He is recognized everywhere as an authority on parliamentary government and the rules. This morning I asked him whether I was correct in my assertion that this type of childish threat had no basis in our parliamentary system. Fortified by his view, I think the majority of the members of this House will now agree that this matter has been brushed aside and no longer requires to be acknowledged even by way of childish condemnation.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, did you ever see such a hodgepodge of legislation together in one bill? This is indeed an example of the degree to which the government brings together a number of subjects which are in no way joined one to the other. This legislation contains some subjects with which the opposition will agree, and others in respect of which the strongest argument can be made to the contrary. Yet we are placed in the position that unless the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North is accepted, we must vote on a bill that contains everything from alpha to omega, all joined together without regard to similarity or any other basic reason.
I will deal with one or two of these matters in an endeavour to bring some light out of the darkness that surrounds that composition. Mr. Speaker, I hope you will

agree with me that this is a wonderful government when it comes to covering up and concealing the truth. It is one of the most interesting phenomena that when members of this government produce their semi-truths and get caught, they fall over, they stumble, they get up and go on as if nothing had happened. That is the position they have adopted throughout. What is this legislation? What is the reason for it?
I have come to the conclusion it is a cover-up to divert the thinking of Canadians from matters such as the mess in which we find the economy, the waste and extravagance of this government which still continues unabated. There is the falling trade, to which reference was made this afternoon, the tremendous deficit in the balance of payments, the industrial anarchy which exists in this country with a government that does not want to act and a government which internationally is suspect all over the free world. In addition, there is the crime which is multiplying. One of the reasons for the dilettante manner in which crime has been treated by this government is the fact that it has been a continual lawbreaker ever since it brought in the legislation which divided murder into two types, noncapital and capital. The Prime Minister, the Solicitor General and others are opposed to capital punishment. They have made that clear.
I have strong views on the subject. When I was prime minister, if a verdict of guilty was rendered and there were no extenuating circumstances or a recommendation of mercy, then, much as I hated to sign what amounted to the death sentence, we followed the law. But this government continues to break the law. Showing the utmost cynicism, the Prime Minister the other day said something like this: "I guess we will have to hang somebody because of public opinion." Could any statement be more cynical?
How will the government implement the gun control sections? I say immediately that I am in entire agreement with the objective, reducing crime by gun. Anyone arguing to the contrary would not have much basis from which to argue. But the means whereby the objective is to be attained, as set out in the bill, indicates a wishy-washy attitude on the part of the government. This plan will not work, and cannot work. It will require a multitude of bureaucrats for registrations and considerations, almost judicial on the part of examining and licensing officers. They will need to discover if the applicant is an alcoholic, if his mind is not as it should be, and so on and so forth. Implementation will require a great deal of examination, and the government knows it.
On page 11 of the little booklet prepared by the combined intelligence of the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General we are told: "It is estimated there are about three million gun users in Canada. Because of this large number, it is intended to phase in the licensing scheme over a three-year period." Let us understand what that means. The government knows that it would take an army of bureaucrats to register. Mind you, thay are not registering guns; the government would not do that. The bureaucrats are to register the individual. The booklet goes on to say: "Various alternatives are being considered including implementation on a region by region basis." That is the first public recognition by this government of regional
April 12, 1976

disparity. Then we are told: "For example, the first year, could see the scheme implemented in Ontario." The registration scheme is to begin here, in Ontario, not in any other part of Canada.
Then we are told that in the following year the scheme will be implemented in western Canada and the territories. Clearly, there is to be open season for guns for a whole year in the western provinces and the territories until the gun law applies to those parts of the country. We are told that in the final year the scheme will be implemented in Quebec and the maritimes.
I have just referred to the last paragraph on page 11 of the "Peace and Security" booklet. Did you ever hear such nonsense? What will be a crime in Ontario in 1976 and part of 1977 will not be a crime elsewhere because the law will apply in Ontario but not to western Canada through to the Pacific coast. There will be no registration requirement there for the first year. There is to be one law for Ontario and a different law for all the other provinces and territories. The paragraph ends with these words:
This breakdown roughly divides the national population into three regional groups. Any implementation scheme would be subject to consultation with the provinces.
I have never seen a more asinine division of responsibility under law than that set out in the pamphlet purporting to deal with questions and answers regarding proposed gun control legislation. The government knows how costly this scheme will be. At first, 900 inspection officers will be needed. Who will pay for them?

Every one who carries or has in his possession a firearm for the purpose of or while committing an indictable offence, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for not less than five years.

When I brought my proposal to the attention of the then minister of justice, who has since been promoted to a higher sphere as Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), he brushed it aside. Dear Sir:
Though you are not my member of Parliament, I am writing to you in the hope, perhaps ingenuous, that the matter of gun control will be subject to a free vote following a rational debate, regardless of the political affiliation of each of you.
The proposal to give bureaucrats the authority to determine who may or may not possess a firearm is an alarming example of the philosophy that "all that is not compulsory must be prohitited." If this measure is to become law, it is not difficult to predict that within a few years firearms in Canada will be restricted to a privileged few and that these arms will all be registered with their serial number. Subsequently it would be easy for a megalomaniac government to seize all rifles under the pretence of emergency measures and therefore secure the submissiveness of the people. If you think that the present government's policy is indeed very moderate and my fears exaggerated and unjustified, or even paranoiac, let me remind you that facism is like cancer: if they are not restrained from the very beginning, they can completely destroy our system.
I do not want to suggest that this government is already on the way to dictatorship, however each time we take one more step towards a larger control by the government we are going towards a future where our children will have no hope.
There is no proof that firearm control can effectively reduce the rate of crime except in a totalitarian state. Of course, with a total lack of freedom and with the support of relentless police forces there is not much violent crime but having lived and worked in some of those peaceful paradises I do not hesitate to take the moderate risks and responsibilities involved in living in a free society even if it is armed.
In its Ottawa Report dated June 20, 1975, the hon. Otto Lang said clearly that

It would be a mistake ... to initiate any legislation ... which would impose unnecessary red-tape upon the law-abiding citizens.

If we force, without logical reason, three of four million Canadians to obtain firearm licences it will merely cause more red tape. In the same report, Mr. Lang admits that the registration of guns will not prevent criminals from obtaining one and will not save the life of those that could be murdered by people who, in the past, have demonstrated no criminal tendency. It seems that the hon. Warren Allmand also accepts such a reality. If the registration of firearms is not beneficial to law and order how, in the name of reason, could the issuance of licences to firearm owners help us? What is the government trying to prove?
I have not had a gun or a rifle for many years but I find it comforting to know that I can buy one as easily as a boy scout hatchet. If my government is not afraid of me, in return I will have no reason to fear that same government. If this moderately repressive measure becomes a law, I will begin getting afraid.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome very much the opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-83. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who took part in the debate earlier this afternoon was at his parliamentary and political best. I would only comment on one reference he made to the effect there has not been consultation with the Wildlife Federation and other groups representing gun owners. The fact is, there has been input from the Wildlife Federation and other groups in respect of this bill. The question is, how much.
We all know very well that consultation today has taken on a somewhat different meaning, depending on who is using the word and what he is speaking about. What most groups are talking about when they say there has been no consultation, or inadequate consultation, is that the group, or whoever it is, has not talked long enough with the government to get it to agree with exactly that group s point of view. If that has not happened, then the charge, of course, is no consultation or inadequate consultation. As I say, that statement of implication by the hon. member was an incorrect one in the sense that there has been consultation, even though the legislation before us may nor coincide with the feelings or the express wishes of the wildlife people. As a matter of fact, in many respects there is not very much difference between the principle put forward by many of the wildlife groups, and others, and that of the government as expressed in this bill.
A great deal has been said-I will probably fall heir to that, too-and many good suggestions have been put forward in this debate. I think the interest displayed, not only by members of the House but as shown in the volume of mail that many of us are receiving from across the country, is indicative of the concern and interest of Canadians in the criminal justice system.
Much of the criticism which has been directed at the bill has been on two fronts: criticism for what is not in the bill, and criticism of some of the provisions that are in the bill, in this case the gun control provisions. The bill has been criticized because it does not deal with drug or alcohol abuse, television violence and half a dozen other fields of genuine concern to a good number of people. On the other hand, it has been criticized because of the seemingly restrictive, all-inclusive nature of some of the provisions relating to gun control. This bill is one of a package put forward by the government to try to meet the very legitimate expressions of concern by Canadians all across the country. In this respect the incidence of crime and violence in this country which, although not as great as, for example, in the United States, is certainly a matter of concern.

The government is not using the fact that our crime rate is below that of the United States and other countries as an inducement for taking no action to meet the concerns of the vast majority of Canadians.
I think Bill C-83 contains some new approaches which our courts and law enforcement people may employ, for example, in dealing with dangerous offenders. I think the legal people in the House and elsewhere can deal with these provisions and, indeed, have dealt with them better than I can, but it seems to me that this is a new approach well worth the consideration and support of members of the House.
I am sure that my constituents are no different from Canadians in other parts of the country in that they are concerned about their own safety and security and that of their families and communities. Generally speaking, their knowledge of the workings of the criminal justice system in this country is based upon local experiences and what they hear and read in the news media as reported from other parts of this country. Here they only hear of the failures of the system. Successes are not reported because they do not make news. For example, the bail system was referred to by the hon. member who preceded me, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). I think the bail system we have in this country is a good case in point, although I realize that this bill does not deal specifically with it. The vast majority of people charged and subsequently released on bail live up to their commitment. They show up for their trial and stay out of trouble in the meantime. It is the 1 per cent or 2 per cent of people who do not which generates apprehension and concern about the entire system in the eyes of the great majority of the public.
In this respect, I am sure many hon. members noted with interest last week a question raised in the House by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). His complaint-quite a legitimate one-related to a constituent of his being held in a Mexican jail without bail for some weeks before his case was even brought to trial. That is the other side of the coin, the other system under which there is no bail at all. Surely it is a much simpler system from the point of view of administration, but it does not constitute what we in Canada consider to be justice. Certainly, human judgment as well as the law itself is very much part of our system. Not only juries, but judges, prosecutors, psychologists and others are continually making personal judgments, not only in sentencing but in granting parole, in rehabilitation of accused persons, as well as in dealing with those already convicted. There are bound to be some errors.
There is a feeling, certainly among my constituents-and in this respect I think they are no different from Canadians elsewhere-that in order to ensure fair treatment of the individual charged with a criminal offence, and even of those convicted, the entire system over the last few years has leaned too far in the direction of protecting the rights of the accused as opposed of the rights of citizens, innocent victims, families thereof, law-abiding citizens, and so on. On the surface, they would appear to be correct in that assumption. I am no lawyer or sociologist, but in listening to and reading reports of people with more experience in crime control, I did not find that I was able to judge
April 12, 1976

whether indeed that is the case. But, as I say, it is a very widely held view that the system does not pay enough attention to the victims of crime.
We have heard in this debate, also, that all we really need is stricter enforcement and application of the present laws. I do not accept that premise in its entirety. I believe, for example, that some of the changes contained in this bill are good and necessary. For example, the parole provisions, the strengthening of the Parole Board, the abolition of statutory parole, the inclusion of local people on the Parole Board when dealing with specific cases, and the inclusion of two people from the community where the offence was committed are good measures and ones that are long overdue.
The wiretapping provisions represent an effort by the government to try to combat organized crime that all of us talk about and all of us lament about; but on the other hand, none of us can really come forward with any specific answers. I am aware of the fact that opinion is divided on the question of expanding the wiretapping provisions, but it seems to me that the essential part here is that strong safeguards be maintained to protect the personal privacy of individuals in this electronic age. I believe that the bill provides that particular assurance.
Provisions dealing with guns have undoubtedly been the subject of greatest controversy. All the present sections of the act dealing with guns and gun control have been written and revised with major new additions in principle. What are the main provisions and principles with which we are dealing in this bill? On the other hand, what are the main concerns that have been expressed to me and other members by the majority of gun owners who are law-abiding citizens?
In his remarks, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) outlined the main provisions of the bill. Firstly, I believe everyone can support higher maximum sentences for most crimes involving guns. Secondly, a mandatory additional sentence of from one to fourteen years for those convicted of using an offensive weapon. I oppose the suggestion put forward earlier by the right hon. member for Prince Albert that a rigid, mandatory five-year sentence be imposed in all cases. I think that one to fourteen years, or two fourteen years-all owing some flexibility-is certainly desirable in a measure of this kind.
Third, the proposal that police have authority to seize weapons without a warrant in an imminently threatening situation deserves the support of all of us. Fourth, the list of prohibited weapons will be enlarged to include such things as sawed-off shotguns. Fifth, there will be a tightening of the present laws with regard to the registration of hand-guns, which we have had for many years. Hand-guns are known as restricted weapons. Sixth, a licensing system is proposed for gun owners which is similar to driver's licences, hunting licences and trapper's licences, which we have had for many years, except that in this case there will have to be two local guarantors, as is now the case with passport applications.
There are provisions and measures in the gun control section of this bill which need to be changed in committee. There are clauses which need to be clarified and clauses
Measures Against Crime
which need to be narrowed in their scope, and their broad application needs to be much more limited. I do not wish at this time to deal with all the clauses which require amendment, but I do not want to touch on some of them.
My major personal criticism of the bill is its structure. I am not satisfied that there is sufficient flexibility in the bill to acknowledge the different traditions which exist in various parts of this country. In this bill dealing with gun control which we will be, and should be, legislating is an umbrella type of law which can be adapted to the traditions which have been established throughout the years in different parts of Canada. It will take two or three years before some of these provisions will be implemented. I suggest that we should give the minister, his staff, provincial attorneys general and others adequate time for provincial and local involvement in the development of regulations which are sensible for every area of the country. In this respect, I suppose we are faced with the age-old and usual Canadian dilemma, namely, developing a bill which fits all areas of our country fairly, a bill which can be tailored to regional and local needs, and a bill which fits not only the north and the south but also the east and west and the rural and urban areas.
The people of my constituency and my province appreciate and understand the need for stricter controls, especially in large urban centres. That is true whether it be in Toronto, Vancouver or Regina. In many respects, guns are too easily accessible; so how do we go about the problem of screening out irresponsible gun owners or those who should not be allowed to buy guns? As hon. members from the province of Saskatchewan are aware, in rural Saskatchewan gun ownership has been part of the country since it was opened up before confederation, just as was the right to own land, to break it and to farm it. These were some of the main reasons many people came to that province from all over the world and from all over the rest of this country. Owning guns has been part of that tradi-dion, whether they were owned for shooting coyotes, gophers, or the old herd bull-to which the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) referred today-with a broken leg out in the pasture. Guns were, and are, part of the normal tools of the trade, just as are plows, saddles and other equipment.
The people in my province and constituency want that tradition maintained. I, personally, believe that the principle of issuing a licence to a gun owner will give him the opportunity to maintain that tradition. In the same way that drivers' licences set out minimum requirements for operating a motor vehicle, surely this system and the principle embodied therein can be made to work. It must be made to work. I agree with the points made by many hon. members of this House, on both sides, that it must be made to work without any great additional bureaucracy and without any great additional expense. In this respect, I feel that the expense should not be borne only by gun owners. We are implementing this provision for the benefit of society as a whole, and all Canadians should help pay for it.
We need some assurances with respect to a number of the clauses in this bill. We need specific answers as to how some of these proposals will be applied. Modifications are

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
required to ensure that some of the legitimate concerns of sportsmen and others are recognized and satisfied.
I should like to take a few minutes to point out that representations from gun owners and sportsmen's groups in this country have not all been entirely critical of this bill. Many have been quite constructive. The Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation is an example of such a group. It is a large, representative and widely dispersed group of gun owners and sportsmen from that province. It is a responsible organization and has already done a great deal to promote safety and training courses in hunting. It has worked to promote greater responsibility in the handling of firearms generally and in training youngsters. They work to promote good conservation practices and good land owner-hunter relationships.
The Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation has examined this bill and enumerated a number of specific objections. I should like to touch on the main ones. First, the federation objects to the licensing system largely because of the great possibility of red-tape. I believe the government can accommodate them in this respect. Second, the federation objects to granting wide powers to the governor in council. Third, with regard to the provision with respect to possible fines or sentences for careless storage and handling of firearms or ammunition, the federation is concerned about the implications and application of this particular clause.
Fourth, it objects to a clause which makes reference to the fact that citizens are bound, under penalty of up to five years, to turn in a report to the police or the local firearms' registrar upon finding an empty cartridge abandoned in a field. If there ever was a nonsense provision in a bill, this has to be it. If there ever was a provision in a bill which would make people uneasy about government bureaucrats, it would be this kind of provision. Certainly, changes must be made.
The fifth point raised by the federation is that under this bill we will not be able to teach or instruct youngsters the basics of gun safety until they are 14 years of age. It will be illegal for anyone under the age of 14 to handle a firearm under any circumstances. I sincerely believe that that limit should be lowered to at least 12 years of age. The 12-year limit is now applied in Saskatchewan and in other provinces. I have a son who took that course three years ago. For the past two years he has been taking cadet courses in this city. He will be 14 this month. It seems to me that we are being unduly restrictive. I support the federation in their objections.
At the same time, to demonstrate their responsibility and concern in the field of gun handling and gun controls, the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation also spelled out its ideas of what would constitute a good, sensible gun control program. It has put forward alternatives to some of the provisions which are in this bill. I ask hon. members to note carefully the great similarity of principle in the points made by the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation and the points aimed for in Bill C-83.
What are the alternatives? The federation suggests the following steps; first, that all persons convicted of violent crime be placed under a lengthy order of prohibition barring them from possessing any firearm; second, that all persons who pose an identifiable threat due to mental instability or alcoholism be placed under a similar order of

prohibition; third, that persons on bail or suspended sentence following arrest or conviction for any violent crime should be prohibited from carrying a firearm, while a person on parole after imprisonment for such a crime might have a similar prohibition imposed as a condition of parole; fourth, that all new hunters and marksmen pass a provincial competence and knowledge test; fifth, that gun dealers be required to keep a record of firearms' sales and open it for police inspection.
The sixth recommendation is that any licensing system designed to cover the sale of firearms and ammunition should be a provincial system with authority to license business operations and sale and purchase transactions. The seventh recommendation is as follows:
That firearms or ammunition be sold, loaned, given, etc., only to a person in possession of either:
(a)	a valid hunting or trapping licence, with several years experience, and competency in firearm's handling or
(b)	a certificate of competency from a recognized firearms' safety course; or
(c)	a membership card from a recognized marksmen's club, or
(d)	a special police permit for a valid requirement not covered by (a), (b), or (c) above;
(e)	land owners.
When one looks at the variety of membership cards and licences referred to there, it seems to me that in the seventh point put forward by the federation one of the alternatives may be some kind of a simplified, universal uniform type of licence.
There are features of this bill which this organization very much supports, such as the banning of fully automatic firearms, increased penalties for the illegal use of firearms, and extended authority to the courts and the police to seize firearms in the interest of safety when serious incidents arise from domestic trouble or mental instability. As I say, this is the kind of constructive criticism we receive from responsible sports and gun clubs in the country.
The Wildlife Federation of Saskatchewan does oppose Bill C-83 in its present form. I support the federation in most of its concerns. Yet it should be obvious to anyone who examines the government's objectives, the federation's objectives and the alternatives, that there really is not that much difference in principle. It is in the method of implementation of those principles that the differences occur. I think the bill has had ample time for debate at the second reading stage.

One final point in respect of this bill which I would like to repeat again is that we need flexibility in respect of the proclamation of the sections relating to the kind of licensing provisions. The proclamation should be on a provincial basis, despite the fun the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) made of that this afternoon.
April 12, 1976

They should be proclaimed in each province when the provincial, municipal and other governments within each province have indicated their readiness, and that full and adequate consultation has taken place with the interested groups to ensure that these provisions are adaptive to the best interests of the people of that particular province.
I think that in general Bill C-83 deserves the support of members and should be sent to the committee where further details can be studied and further very necessary amendments can be made to the several clauses of the bill which require consideration.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the strictest security failed to save the lives of several United States presidents, writes Frank Arnie from Preeceville, Saskatchewan, a constituent of mine. I think he summarizes in one little sentence what many of us think. I have followed this debate very carefully in this House.
The bulk of the concern in respect of Bill C-83 is with reference to the gun legislation. This is the particular section about which I am concerned. I would like to separate the other sections so far as surveillance is concerned. The people who live in rural areas know all about surveillance, having party lines. In many parts of my area the people do not even have a telephone; they still use the radio to communicate from one community to another, and everybody listens in.
This legislation which has been drafted by a bunch of city slickers for the conditions in the cities will do nothing but harass the rural areas. It may be valid in respect of the metropolitan areas of Toronto and Montreal. As my friend from the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) said, "My God; do I ever see a need for it in Montreal!" We must understand the real danger in trying to apply a set of laws drafted by city people who have probably never lived outside the city limits and who have no idea what rural life is like.
I think the government has lost its credibility in respect of running this country. It does not have the pulse of the nation; it does not know what the people really want. As the member who just spoke said, this is umbrella-type legislation. I know that time will never allow me to say the many things I want to say in objection to this piece of legislation, particularly as it applies to gun control.
As I said, I have listened to this debate very intently. I listened to the speech of the Creditiste member, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau). When he made his remarks, I said to myself that I could endorse what he had to say. His concern had to do with the registration of guns and the affect this had had in central Europe and Cuba where governments have been overthrown because of the confiscation of weapons and because of registration. Perhaps I should also mention Russia, because I have been to Russia and I could tell a story that would make your hair stand on end about how I was treated by the bureaucracy there. Mr. Speaker, one might say that that cannot happen here. I know the type of concern the people have, because I have been to Russia. The local registrar could become the local commissar. This is the kind of thing I am concerned about because of my own personal experience, not because I have read it.
I have referred to the speech of the hon. member for Shefford. Now I should like to refer to the speech made by
Measures Against Crime
the member of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). I wish to endorse entirely his comments. My area adjoins his territory. I have northern people in my riding; I have northern Indian settlements. The situation in my area is entirely different from the situation in the cities. I have trappers and I have fishermen. In the middle of the winter, if one goes ice-fishing one carries a gun.
Now I should like to go to the government side of the House and say that I endorse almost entirely the speech made by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) except for the one point where he came to the conclusion that perhaps this type of restriction would help curb the incidence of crime. I understand the situation in respect of the sad case we had here in Ottawa. I know the people of Ottawa are now pretty well convinced that gun control is required in order to prevent similar instances.
From a reading of the brief presented by the Alberta Wildlife Federation, I understand that that poor lad in his sad frame of mind broke at least four firearms' laws which presently are on the books. Will additional laws solve the problem? I tell you, in all sincerity, that additional laws would not have prevented that tragic incident. I mention it because the government emphasizes too much what additional laws may achieve.
This second reading debate is to end with closure. Why are the gun provisions wrong, Mr. Speaker? We have heard that you have to be a chairman, president, active or retired, to be considered. I tell you, not many farmers belong to gun clubs. Not many trappers belong to gun clubs. For them, the gun is an essential tool. You must distinguish between the man who uses his gun occasionally for pleasure and the man who needs it as a tool. Some people might take their guns out once a year to go trap-shooting. In my area we do not go trap-shooting; we shoot muskrat. Our youngsters learn how to use guns. I first used a gun when I was about 12. I was much younger than my counterparts in the city who might use guns. Occasionally I brought home supper, partridges or jackrabbits. Occasionally we had rabbit stew. I carried a gun when I was 12. Our youngsters learn to respect a gun. I earned my first 15 cents when I went into the bush near our pasture to shoot some bush rabbits. They were fetching five cents each. I walked four miles into town to make 15 cents. The situation in our rural parts is not the same as in the city.
The same bunch who drafted this bill will be responsible for drafting regulations. And do not tell me you can change a bill in committee. I remember what the former minister of Justice, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, did to some proposals I brought forward. I proposed some amendments in the agriculture committee and they were acceptable to the committee, but the minister who accepted them reversed his position. He would not accept the amendments I proposed in committee and they were voted down in the House. Therefore, do not tell me his committee members reverse themselves. How easy it is to change a bill in committee!
This situation reminds me of a child at table. The mother says, "Eat your borsch," and the child says, "But, momma, I don't like the beans." If the mother allowed the child to

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
separate the beans from the rest of the soup, all would be well. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) is saying just that. He is saying, "We like the soup, but don't like the beans. Why do you not let us put the beans to one side?" He wants the beans to be separated from the soup. In the case of the child, if the mother agrees and the beans are taken out, the child can eat the soup and absorb the nourishment. If she does not agree and makes the child swallow the beans, the child can bring up, and it will be pretty messy.
The government is trying to create a mess. We can eat beans, of course, but not everything is digested. We absorb what is good. We shall absorb the good parts of this bill and you will hear no more about it. But after we eat, there is some excretion. If I know this government, it will either leave it alone, or flush it down. This legislation reminds me of the digestive process, because just as hydrochloric acid does not break down all foods ingested, so the committee system as now set up will not enable us to extract from the bill what is bad and unnecessary. This little parable is meant to show you that it is impossible to refine; you will not end up with good legislation.
As I said before, the hon. member for Shefford made a fine speech. He was concerned about the registration program. All must register, but nobody knows the regulations. Nobody seems to be much worried about them. The government merely says, "Register." That brings to mind my experience in Russia. I could tell you stories that would make your hair stand on end. I was holed up in a little hotel in a small village. They had an administration there, and I was dragged before a kangaroo court. They tried to hold me there. That was all part of the workings of bureaucracy. Then the army was alerted at the railway station and soldiers ran up to my compartment with fixed bayonets. Yes, this all happened to me. I am not telling you something I heard; it actually happened to me.
I have a friend in Endeavour, Saskatchewan, by the name of A. J. Kobe. In May of this year he sent me a document which reads in part as follows:
In May of 1919 at Dusseldorf, Germany, the allied forces obtained a copy of some of the 'Communist Rules for Revolution.' Nearly 50 years later, the reds are still following them. After reading the list, stop after each item and think about the present day situation where you live- and all around our nation-
The first item on the list is this:
A.	Corrupt the young, get them away from religion. Get them interested in sex-
Television is doing a good job in that area. I continue:
B.	Get control of all means of publicity, thereby:
1.	Get people's minds off their government by focusing their attention
on athletics ...
2.	Divide the people into hostile groups ...
3.	Destroy the people's faith in their natural leaders ...
4.	Always preach true democracy ...
6. Incite unnecessary strikes ... encourage civil disorders-
I draw attention particularly to paragraph C, which says:
Cause the registration of all firearms on some pretext, with a view to confiscating them and leaving the population helpless.
That document came to light in 1919. Deny that what it recommends could not happen here. Will any say it could not happen here? Do you remember what happened in the

Quebec crisis? All who owned guns were willing to give them up. All would have been willing to register if there had been provisions for registration. We were told there was an apprehended insurrection. Then we discovered that the trouble-makers were few in number and most of them ended up in Cuba. That is the place our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) visited recently and, boy, was he ever chummy with Castro. He was so close to Castro that you did not know which was the one with natural hair or which was the one who wished he had some. That shows how chummy they were. And you say it couldn't happen here!
I remember when the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) acted in a different capacity. He set up what was later referred to as the Goyer goon squad: he set up what amounted to a parallel police force. I know that the Prime Minister, despite the protests of the former minister of finance, set up a sort of parallel government. People tell me, "Watch this man." I am saying this because I have watched him and drawn my own conclusions. Yes, people tell me, "Watch this man; he is dangerous." Now the government wants a central registry of guns. I say, watch it! They say it could not happen here. Remember what happened in central Europe, Russia and Cuba? When I was in Europe I thought it was sad to have soldiers standing in front of public buildings. I thought, "Thank God I live in a better country." Several years later I found the same situation in this country. Ministers were being protected by military men with guns. Given the right set of circumstances, it can happen here.
My time is rapidly moving on. There are many things I would like to say. I will, however, make this proposal. If registration is necessary, it should be by enabling legislation, enabling each province to register. The provinces should be given that right. I know that provinces have given some rights to the federal government, the federal government has given certain rights to them, and so on. Therefore, it is possible to give the provinces the right to register. In that way there would at least not be a central registry. Even though there is a daily erosion, the preservation of democracy is important. By having registration in the various provinces it will be up to them to draw their own regulations and apply them as conditions warrant. Segregate the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Some of those people have had certain freedoms provided to them over the years.
The explanatory note is a farce; it is phony. It makes me sick to think that people are being led to believe there will be a measure of protection. For the record, I think the explanation should read as follows:
A bill to provide for registration and confiscation of guns; the provisions for a licence for murder; the creation of a bureaucracy and for greater protection of the government;
Further, to provide the illusion of security and the removal of certain freedom to natives provided under the Treaty of Paris;
The implementation of certain laws to equate the law-abiding citizen with the criminal element;
The implementation of laws which will guarantee an increase in lawbreakers.
That is the way the explanatory note should read, because that will be net effect. I have mentioned the
April 12, 1976

Creditistes and the NDP. I endorse the speech made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) as well as that made by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) with regard to the absurdity that will exist if this type of regulation is put into effect.
If you start with the wrong principle, I do not see how in the world it can then be improved by sending it to committee. I am going to have to make a decision with regard to this bill. I feel very strongly about it. In so doing, I want to remind every newspaper man and commentator in this country that I am not opposing my party. My party does not have anything to do with this bill. I am opposing a stupid piece of legislation. I want to be able to separate the beans from the rest. I have that right. As Richard Lovelace said:
Stone walls do not a prison make,
Nor irons bars a cage;
Minds innocent and quiet take That for an hermitage;
My party does not inhibit me. That is the kind of thing that happens. Too many times there is a wrong answer by the wrong person on the wrong thing. Given the power of their persuasion in the media, they often make a big thing out of nothing, and nothing out of a big thing.
I said that this bill was drafted by a bunch of city slickers for city conditions. In all the years I have walked the streets of the city, outside of a police officer I have never seen a man carrying a gun. However, I have seen a lot of people in rural areas carrying guns. I have never seen a patrol car in the city stopping a series of cars, but in the rural areas they stop you to check your driver's licence, brakes, lights and that sort of thing. The only time that is done in the city is when there is a traffic violation. Therefore, you can see where the harassment will be. The cities want this legislation. It is the rural people who will be harassed by it.
I will sum up in a few words what I think is going to happen. I could draw several parallels. No one thinks that a gun is a necessary tool for the farmer. A gun is required for humane slaughter. City slickers have never seen a pig being slaughtered; they would not know how it is done. You take careful aim with a .22 and fire a shot at the middle of the pig's forehead. That stuns it. You can then proceed to slaughter. You leave your gun while slaughtering. You do not have time to carry the gun to relative safety. After 1 Vi or 2 hours you are finished a with a good job. You then go in to wash up. If a police officer had come along and seen the gun and the shells, in the course of his duty he would have had to charge the farmer because the gun was not carefully stored.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for this opportunity to continue. I was illustrating the kind of situation that could be found in a rural area and why it is absolutely essential to have a gun for humane slaughter.
I now wish to deal with another situation. If any kind of a licence is to be granted, it should be a family licence because at one time or another every member of the family will be expected to use that gun. Suppose the father owns the gun and you give him a licence. You don't give the father the right to murder everybody else, and you don't give the others an equal chance. He's got to have the key. A gun on a farm is a tool.

Measures Against Crime
I don't know whether members have ever seen what happens when a fox or coyote walks in among a flock of turkeys or hens. He doesn't grab one and run off with it, as city fellows might think. He grabs one and jumps the next one, and cripples the next one and goes to 15 or 20 of them, crippling them. Then, having crippled them, knowing they cannot get away from him he proceeds to haul them out one by one and he buries them. That is something a lot of these city slickers don't know.
You've got to keep a gun handy. You need a gun on a farm, and every member of the family has to be able to use that gun at any time. Suppose an animal is crippled and the father who has the gun is away. He may be away and he is the only one who has the right to buy any shells. If you have an animal, a horse or a cow with a broken leg, nobody dare go into town and get any shells. First of all, it is illegal; you cannot buy shells if you haven't got a licence, nor should the store operator sell them.
Why shouldn't everybody have a licence? After all, it is a family gun. It is a possession necessary for the entire family. What do you do in a situation such as I have described? Do you let the animal suffer, or do you break the law? Obviously, you are going to break the law and there is an invitation to break the law.
A whole lot of farmers and ranchers travel from one farm to the other; their land is scattered all over the place and they carry their .22 in a half-ton truck. They do so because they know that coyotes have been known to attack calves. Then, again, our country is bear country and bears are known to carry off calves. That is why a gun is always carried around. There are predators. A skunk could get into a chicken-run. All kinds of situations could develop. I can visualize a situation in which a farmer, having made his rounds, goes home and sits down to eat dinner. He is in a hurry-farmers are always in a hurry because there is always work to do. While he is there, the hired man comes in and says, "There is a breakdown somewhere." The farmers says, "Take the truck quick and drive into town to get the parts. The hired man dashes into the truck and heads out. On the way to town he meets a patrol car with a bubble-gum machine on top. The officers stop him and asks to see his licence. They want to check his brakes. While looking around the truck, they see the gun. The following conversation takes place, "Can we see your licence for that gun?" "I do not have one". "Oh, you haven't got a licence." Trouble, trouble! Mr. Speaker, the people who drafted this legislation have no idea what rural life is like.
Have you ever seen a trapper come off the trap lines? Have you ever seen the fishermen come off the ice in winter after fishing? They carry their guns. The kids carry their guns. What is a trapper going to do? He carries his gear in, dumps it into one corner, and there is the gun. Do you think the first thing he does before he even shakes the snow from his back is to lock up that gun? How ridiculous can we be? You have to go into these rural areas to understand. The people who drew up this legislation have no idea what it is like. How are we going to improve on this sort of thing in committee, when it is all based on the wrong premise? You are drawing up legislation oblivious of the fact that there is a rural part of Canada.

I say, Oh, my gosh, you can do that in the city areas, "though I don't know what good it is. "If you want it in the cities, you can have it. But don't tamper with us, don't tamper with our work." The Indian has a right, under the Treaty of Paris, to have that gun. The white man has done it once again-gone out there and tampered with his rights and freedom.
I shall go on to something else which ought to be considered. The Indian population of this country is 1.37 per cent of the whole, yet the percentage of the Indian population incarcerated in our jails is 8.37 per cent. Obviously, this is some sort of record. But what kind of prison record will make it impossible under this legislation for a man to own a gun? In many cases the sentences involved here are short sentences. We have to bear in mind that a large percentage of the native population is in and out of jail. Is the minister telling me, then, that he intends to deny the right of every one of those men to own a gun because of some sort of prison record? I don't know. Nothing is spelled out in the bill as we see it before us. How much leeway have we got? You ask us to buy a pig in a poke, or a cat in a bag-whatever it is-and then you turn around and say, "It is good, because for the sake of political propaganda this is what we are going to do."
I want to go on to one other thing. I said this bill will set up a bureaucracy. It seems to me that if you want to register guns, it ought not to be necessary to go back and do it again five years later. The only reason I can see for that is the need to pay for this bureaucracy once it has been set up. I am told it might cost as much as $30 for a gun licence; that is one estimate that has been made. Can you imagine a father with two sons having to pay $90 between them for these licences?
My .22 only cost me $11 to begin with. One of my constituents wrote to me saying that his father bought his .22 for $4.95. To pay licence fees at this level is ridiculous. Obviously, there have to be exemptions here. After five years, you have to go back to the same official to re-register. Why? What happens if you have one gun and three members of a family, for example, the father and two sons, register; or, for that matter, a mother, if she is inclined to shoot at all? Nothing is spelled out. Where do you draw the line? Suppose there is one member of a family who is unstable? Is that family barred from having a gun? I don't know. Nothing is indicated in the bill. The only justification I can see for going back after five years is that the government, having set up a huge bureaucracy, must somehow raise the money to pay for it. Of course, we all know who is going to pay for it. It is the gun owner-it doesn't matter if the gun only cost $5 to buy originally.
Mr. Speaker, I am told by my whip that I have only about one minute left. I wish I had more time. I can only say one thing. In the words of the Alberta Wildlife Federation, Bill C-83 is "One Basford of a bill".

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was speaking this afternoon he congratulated the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), who is the justice critic recently appointed by the new leader of his party and was also the justice
April 12, 1976

critic of his party under the former leader, on his sixtieth birthday. Might I also add my congratulations. I have always found him to be co-operative and helpful when as chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs from time to time over a period of many months we were organizing the appearance of witnesses before the committee.
The hon. member for Calgary North, relatively recently-I believe on May 30, 1975-in a question directed to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) asked when the government was going to bring forth for examination a bill to restrict the ownership of certain guns and control others. This bill has been brought forth by the government as part of its peace and security package at the request not only of the hon. member and others but of attorneys general across Canada. Hon. members will remember that very recently the attorney general of the province of Ontario indicated that if legislation to restrict and control the ownership of guns in this country was not brought forward by this government, he intended to do so himself.
When speaking earlier today, the right hon. gentleman also complained of lack of consultation with certain important groups in this country before the legislation was brought forward. He mentioned the former commissioner of the RCMP, who I believe is now associated with the Canadian Wildlife Federation. As a matter of fact, the former commissioner, Mr. Nicholson, was consulted in detail when he presented a brief last June to the Solicitor General and to other interested parties at the time this legislation was being drafted. My understanding is that some 80 per cent of the matters raised by Mr. Nicholson on behalf of the Canadian Wildlife Federation were considered and in fact included in the legislation.
The justice committee has always been receptive to the representations of all parties who have interested positions to present on legislation before it. I would commend, as do many members on this side of the House, that we move this bill into committee for in-depth and detailed study of all its clauses.
As the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) said-and as is so obvious-there are, of course, differences in respect of controlling and using guns between rural areas of Canada and urban areas. I agree with the Canadian Wildlife Federation, other groups interested in the use and control of firearms and with the point of view of other members of the House that the committee could entertain, if the hon. member would so submit, the type of amendment that he feels would satisfy the complaints he made regarding certain incidents, such as having one gun in the family and perhaps five people having access to it in order to protect their assets on the farm, animals and so on. Such an amendment ought to be considered by the committee.
The minister also indicated that he is prepared to listen to any representations in connection with amendments which are put forward with reason and logic, so we can show that we can provide Canadians with some degree of protection against the misuse of firearms, not only the use of firearms to commit criminal offences but also in regard to the tragic accidents that have been occurring, in some cases through lack of understanding and knowledge of proper storage.
Measures Against Crime
Unlike the hon. member for Mackenzie who has had the good fortune to live in the country, these people have had no training in the use of weapons. To the hon. member for Mackenzie these weapons are like any other tool that is used on the farm and in farming communities. People who live in cities and move to the country do not have this kind of familiarization with weapons. In their hands, they sometimes become very dangerous, not because of any intention on their part to commit crime but because of their lack of understanding of their use. Indeed, they have probably never had an opportunity to use a firearm.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert also said there were some on this side, though he did not name them, who do not like the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In my years in parliament, Mr. Speaker, I have not been able to detect any such feeling. In fact, I have detected, on the contrary, a great sense of pride and, yes, sense of security that we have in our Royal Canadian Mounted Police force, one of the most efficient police forces in the world.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
I suggest they are one of the most respected international police forces. I would point out to the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert that an indication of this is the fact that the former commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is now president of Interpol. To indicate, or by innuendo suggest that there are some on this side who do not like the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is to cast an unfair shadow on the great work and integrity of that force, from their senior officers right down through the ranks, and I think that ought not to go unanswered.
I believe the Solicitor General-it is an honour for me to work with him-has a mandate to work on behalf of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in parliament and he has been doing that job effectively and well. I know he considers the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, in representing them in this House and in committees of the House, second to none and places them before many of his other concerns. One of the reasons for this is, of course, this peace and security package that is now before the House.
Several hon. members have spoken in the debate so far and made points to which I should like briefly to refer. For example, in his speech in this debate the hon. member for New Wesminster (Mr. Leggatt) made several important points about the causes of crime. One point which he stressed concerned the disproportionate number of native Canadians who are presently incarcerated in Canada. He went on to state that it is essential to approach the problem of crime at its roots in order to make progress toward preventing such an intolerable situation from persisting into the future. I cannot agree more with the hon. member. That is why certain initiatives have been taken by the federal government outside the context of this bill to approach the very problem which he mentioned.
In order to meet this problem, a major conference of native leaders and federal and provincial ministers was held in Edmonton just over a year ago. This conference of native people and the law explored the problem which was touched on by the hon. member and determined that a follow-up structure should be established in order to pursue solutions to these problems. The federal govern-

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
ment is now moving ahead with the native advisory councils created as a result of that conference.
Just a few weeks ago in Montreal a meeting of the Canadian advisory council on native people and the law was held. This council consists of representatives of the federal and provincial governments and provincial governments and the leaders of the six major native organizations across the country. One specific project, which deals with the concerns expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster, is the program of the federal advisory council on native people and the law to work very closely with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to develop training programs for all recruits to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in order that a more effective approach to the policing of native communities in Canada can be implemented.
Within the ministry of the Solicitor General it is recognized that more native people are required within the criminal justice system and, as a result of that, a study has recently been completed examining ways in which this can be implemented. Within the penitentiaries we have expanded the use of native liaison officers and also made great progress in utilizing native service programs in order to help our native inmates. Furthermore, recommendations flowing from the Edmonton conference concerning the creation of work camps and the transfer of native inmates to provincial institutions closer to their homes have been pursued and will continue to be followed up.
Programs by other departments designed to get at the very roots of the criminal problem in our native communities have also been established. One of the important programs of this type is the joint program of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and National Health and Welfare. I am referring to the National native alcohol abuse program which has been funded at a level of $13 million over the next three years and is aimed at getting at the very roots of crime which so often are related to alcohol abuse among our native people.
In concluding then, Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure you that the government recognizes that the concerns expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster are very real and very important, and that the government is taking action designed to get at the problems which are the source of these concerns. If there are no specific amendments to this bill, that does not mean the federal government is inactive in this field.
As many authorities point out, including the Law Reform Commission, real changes in the criminal justice system do not necessarily come from changes in law alone but also from improvements in programs, training, administration, and so on. I think some of the examples I have mentioned show that the federal government is deeply concerned and is in fact actively pursuing solutions in this area.
The legislation has also been questioned by hon. members on the grounds that it does not contain specific provisions to deal with the hard drug problem in this country. The government fully appreciates the seriousness of this problem and places a high priority on it. It was pointed out that there is a strong statistical relationship between the

traffic in hard drugs and violent crime in Canada. I agree with this. But it would be a mistake to look at the measures now before us for the ultimate solution to this serious and complex problem. The legislation cannot be expected to solve all problems of crime.
Strict provisions for dealing with illegal importation and traffic in hard drugs are in the Narcotic Control Act. The RCMP and other police forces across the country have placed a high priority on enforcing these provisions. When we discuss the treatment of heroin addicts, however, we begin to see the enormous complexities and the difficulties which must be faced. As hon. members know, the government did not implement the Le Dain commission's recommendation for compulsory treatment. Hon. members are surely aware, however, the recommendation concerning treatment was not directed at the federal government but at the provinces who are responsible for programs of this sort. The federal government has an important role to play in supporting and faciliting changes that might be introduced, but I think it is significant that no provincial authority has yet advocated the adoption of the commission's proposal.
On the question of a national drug maintenance system for addicts, which was also mentioned, a federal maintenance program designed to ensure the most effective use for methadone in the treatment of opiate dependence has been in operation for over four years now. In the Ministry of the Solicitor General funds are provided to assist community rehabilitation centres working in this field as well. No less than two chapters of the Le Dain commission's final report were devoted to this problem and the government has taken the benefit of much of the commission's advice in this respect.
Experience with deprivation of liberty as a means of facilitating treatment and rehabilitation of drug addicts has not been encouraging. The experience with treatment in prison settings has been definitely unsatisfactory, with virtually all studies demonstrating a very high rate of relapse and recidivism. In response to this awareness, the proportion of persons found in illegal possession of heroin who have been placed on probation in the community on condition of compliance with a treatment program increased from 10 per cent in 1969 to 29 per cent in 1974. In many cases a condition of probation has been that the offender participate in and co-operate with a federally-approved methadone maintenance program. In this respect the government and the courts have been involved in the implementation of the Le Dain commission's recommendation for increased use of probation for heroin addicts on condition that they comply with an approved treatment program.
I have dealt at some length with these matters to show not only that the government shares the concern about these problems but also that it is moving on several united fronts to deal with them. Again, however, it is important that we separate the problems associated with the traffic in drugs and the treatment of drug addicts from the specific problems dealt with in the legislation now before us.
In this debate on the crime prevention bill, I could sum up my position in the following way. The government is proposing measures in this bill, and in another bill which will shortly be considered by the House, in order to further
April 12, 1976

the goal in affording a better measure of protection for the Canadian public against crime and to make our laws more equitable and humane. The government is taking the approach that certain parts of the criminal law can be tightened up in order to effect that goal. At the same time, however, other proposals of a legislative, regulatory and administrative nature in this package, some of which have been touched on today and other days, help to humanize the criminal justice system. I am referring specifically to the measure to introduce more due process into parole matters, to widen the community input into the parole process, and so on. A central theme in all this is the stress that must be put on the "front-end" of the criminal justice system; on efforts to prevent crime from occurring in the first place. Our goal is the establishment of measures which will be more effective in protecting the public.
It is my contention that each and very one of the measures presented in this bill, and in the peace and security package generally, can stand on its own feet and can meet the test of effectiveness which has been proposed as the benchmark against which the peace and security package should be measured. Furthermore, it is most important that the House understand that this bill and the peace and security package as a whole be considered as part of an ongoing process.
I believe that this crime prevention bill presented by my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), is a worthy next step to the one taken by this House in passing Bill C-71, and that the bill currently before us should be seen in this light. It is also important to remind ourselves that efforts continue on other problems as well. I refer to the examination of the Law Reform Commission's reports on criminal justice matters and the current series of nationwide consultations upon new legislation affecting young offenders.
The measures in this bill and in the peace and security package as a whole are also the product of a lengthy process of study within the federal government and of consultation with the provinces and private groups. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has chaired two full-scale federal-provincial conferences on corrections, one in December, 1973, in Ottawa and the other in May, 1975, in Victoria. The Minister of Justice also meets regularly with his provincial counterparts, and he and the Solicitor General met with attorneys general and provincial ministers of justice on two occasions last fall alone. In addition, there has been set up a continuing committee of deputy ministers on corrections which has met on several occasions in the recent past. The latest meeting of deputy attorneys general was held here in Ottawa a few weeks ago.
In outlining these continuing forums for consultation, I should also mention other meetings such as the meeting of firearms' registrars last June, the conference and follow-up meetings on native people and the law held in the past year, and continuing discussions with private groups such as the Canadian Criminology and Corrections Association and the John Howard and Elizabeth Fry societies. From this you can see that the federal government is most serious about consultation with other authorities responsible for the criminal justice system in Canada.
Some of the important measures proposed in this bill are the amendments with respect to electronic surveillance.
Measures Against Crime
The police experience since the bill was passed in 1974, the Protection of Privacy Act, is that each and every one of these proposed amendments is necessary in order to provide the police with the most up to date and modern methods to be used in detecting and combating crime and organized criminals. The bill provides that rather than those enumerated now, all indictable offences will be subject to wiretapping in the event a court order is obtained.
Also, the act, if these provisions are accepted by parliament, will be generally amended to provide and act which will be almost identical to those introduced by the government in 1973. The amendments which were advocated by hon. members opposite at that time, and which were adopted, I believe have been shown through police experience to be a mistake. By notifying the person whose conversation has been intercepted within 90 days after the tapping has been completed we are not doing anything to tamper with the civil liberties of individuals. What we are doing in a positive way is to place an alarm bell in the offices of individuals implicated in organized crime telling them that the police of this country, who have obtained a warrant to detect them in this manner, know where they are and what their operations are, but have not yet been successful in obtaining enough evidence to carry a case on to prosecution.
The ordinary, small time criminal will not be very impressed with the notification that his telephone was bugged, if information was obtained although there was not sufficient information to lay a charge, but people involved in organized crime look upon such an alarm bell placed in their office as a tremendous bonus to each of them in all their endeavours.
If this bill is accepted, the return of evidence, directly or indirectly obtained is, I believe, a proper restoration of the common law procedure which we have used in this country based on the English common law system that, if evidence is admissible in a court, evidence which indicates the truth of a series of actions, it ought to be admitted so that the jury and the judge will have all the credible evidence before them in order to determine the guilt or innocence of the prosecuted party. This is a proper step. If there is any illegality in obtaining that evidence, or any other evidence that is usually submitted to a court, appropriate action can be taken with regard to anyone who would resort to such a method to get evidence for a trial.
In closing I should like to commend to the House the bill before us as a reasonable piece of legislation and a necessary and effective step in ensuring that our criminal justice system is made a more responsive, more adaptive, and more effective tool to improve the quality of Canadian life. I would also like to stress again the words of the Minister of Justice when opening this debate when he made it clear he was open to proposals for improvements in the bill.
I think it is clear to all who have studied the criminal justice system that the criminal law is really only one of the control mechanisms in our society, and the criminal justice system is only one of several systems. But in its widest definition, the criminal justice system includes everyone in our society, and it is also a reflection of what we are and what we value.

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
Because this implies more than just law enforcement or crime prevention, the quality of the criminal justice system, which we all understand cannot be perfect, depends upon the quality of the individual and the quality of the community-upon the degree or integrity, selfrespect, and the sense of public responsibility for which we all must strive. For this reason I am convinced that answers to the important problems of crime in our society will not be found by experts alone, and that it is the business and even the duty of all law abiding Canadians to bring their contribution to bear on this formidable task.
