speechtext:
Hon. members opposite are the ones who have to answer, not me. I am in the opposition. Is this illicit activity, which this Liberal government allows to grow like poppies in Turkey, an excuse for a larger and larger law enforcement bureaucracy? More bureaucracy on bureaucracy, and I ask, why doesn't an act for the better protection of Canadian society against perpetrators of violent and other crime include legislation for the registration of narcotic addicts and remove from society those addicts who will not accept and abide by a proper, just, sensible, and humane rehabilitative program? This would remove the profit motive which is behind 70 per cent of all crime in Canada, instead of fooling around with this malaise of nonsense we have in Bill C-83. Nothing would make a more meaningful contribution to peace and security in Canada than legislation in this area of need.
In introducing this bill the Minister of Justice stated that "the central objective of Bill C-83, the government's peace and security program, can be simply stated-it is to counter rising violence in our society without resort to violence itself in response, this to the end that law abiding citizens will know a greater degree of security and safety while still preserving that critical balance in the scales of justice."
There are clauses in Bill C-83 which in fact, attempt to serve the central objectives stated by the Minister of Justice. I do not have the benefit of a formal education in law but I am from the street and have a concern which is shared by many out there.
There are five or six aspects of this bill which I favour, and in saying this I am perfectly content to entrust the examination and improvement of these aspects to the wisdom of my colleagues in the committee.
One of the aspects I refer to is the dangerous offenders category which repeals the existing section of the Criminal Code dealing with habitual criminals and dangerous sexual offenders. I welcome this new provision which will allow the courts to impose indeterminate sentences of imprisonment of dangerous offenders.
The second provision which I am in favour of is the maximum penalty for escape or attempted escape, and I particularly favour the repeal of statutory remission, which is to be replaced with earned remission.
The third provision I favour is that provinces will be given the authority to create special commissions of inquiry into organized crime which will give the provinces the legal power to call witnesses and documents from other provinces.
The fourth provision for which I have sympathy is the extension of wiretapping authority from the present 30 days to 60 days. I believe this is a valuable aid to law enforcement because statistics show that the average period of need has been 54.1 days. Most breaks in major
Measures Against Crime
crime, and particularly in narcotic distribution, have been through this valuable law enforcement aid.
A fifth aspect, which on the surface appears to go in the right direction, is the provision for the management of parole services to be transferred to the Commission of Corrections and for the number of board members to be increased to 26 permanent members. I am hopeful that the committee will give full consideration to allowing the sentencing judge discretion in the assessment of individual parole cases.
I am also sympathetic to the search and seizure provisions because I feel that the time is past for legislators to consider safety and other factors affecting the morale of law enforcement officers. It is my opinion that these six initiatives carried in Bill C-83 are valuable, and I have no difficulty agreeing with them in principle. As I stated, I leave their perfection and improvement to the wisdom of my colleagues who are trained in this regard.
This brings me to the point of concern and mistrust I have for the authors of this legislation. Rather than move forward with meaningful measures to correct our law and assist our law enforcement agencies, they turn this very serious subject into a three ring political circus by devoting 39 of 73 pages to the highly emotional subject of gun control.
Gun control is a subject which deserves full and open debate on its own, and that is why I urge hon. members on the government side to support the very wise amendment which was allowed to be put by Mr. Speaker to the second reading motion of this bill.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Just in case hon. members opposite do not understand the amendment, I will read it. It proposes that:
Bill C-83 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for the purpose of considering a more proper legislative division thereof.
According to the Minister of Justice, the gun control measures proposed in Bill C-83 are of a "comprehensive nature directed both to those who would use guns for criminal purposes and to others who, in using them for legitimate ends, must learn to do so with greater respect and care." Yet the minister immediately tries to clarify the matter for us by saying that, "for those who use firearms as tools of their criminal trade no registration and licensing system will effectively curb continued access to and use of weapons." The minister admits that gun controls will not affect the availability of weapons to the criminal elements of society but instead will compel law abiding citizens to create another bureaucracy so that those who own guns can be licensed and their names kept on a list. For what purpose? It is not the gun which kills, it is the will behind the gun.
We have all been inundated with statistics, but I offer a few which show that anti-gun laws do not get at the real problem and do not affect homicide rates. One example is Switzerland where every man over 18 is trained and required to possess and maintain a firearm in his home. In 1968 the homicide rate in Switzerland was 0.7 per 100,000

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
population. On the other hand, in Japan, which prohibits civilian ownership of firearms, the homicide rate was 2.3 in 1968. It is interesting to note that in Switzerland there is a mandatory weapon sentence to be served consecutively with sentences for crimes. In addition, Swiss correctional institutions are self supporting, and when you are a visitor in them, you work.
Does licensing work? The same statistics, provided by the government, point out that 68.4 per cent of all firearm murders resulting from criminal acts are committed with handguns, and handguns are licensed under present laws. The fact is that crimes of violence will continue to be committed, with or without firearms. From 1961 to 1974, 44.2 per cent of all victims were murdered by firearms, and 55.8 per cent were murdered by other means.
It is my contention that crimes of passion will continue to be committed, because they are usually committed by people who are not chronic criminals. If guns are not available, other means will be used. It is my belief that many of the people involved in this class of tragedy would not have trouble being registered or licensed because before the event many would be considered normal citizens. Crime cannot and will not be controlled by placing undue restrictions on law abiding citizens, as the gun control measures in Bill C-83 attempt to do.
Why this new legislation when our present law, if enforced, would do the job? For instance, under the present code section 83 makes it an indictable offence liable to imprisonment for five years to carry a weapon for a purpose dangerous to the public peace, or for the purpose of committing an indictable offence. Surely people committing crimes while in possession of a firearm can also be charged with that, in addition to the offence committed under this section of the code. Why is it not being enforced? If there are problems of interpretation, why do we not amend this section?
Section 85 of the present code makes it an indictable offence, liable to imprisonment for five years, to carry a concealed weapon without a permit. What person who is going to commit a crime would not conceal his weapon, and how many of these weapons are actually registered? Again the person who has committed a crime while in possession of a weapon could also be charged under this section of the code. To my knowledge this is not being done. If it is being done, it is not being done consistently.
Under section 86 of the Criminal Code any one who, "without lawful excuse, points at another person a firearm, whether loaded or unloaded, or uses, carries or possesses any firearm or ammunition in a manner dangerous to the safety of other persons, is guilty of an indictable offence" and liable to two years' imprisonment or is guilty of on offence punishable on summary conviction.
Any person committing a crime while in possession of a firearm could be considered possessing a firearm in a manner dangerous to the safety of other persons. Why are criminals who are that the new proposed gun control measures are redundant and are merely duplicating the functions of the aforementioned sections of the Criminal Code. It is convenient, conventional wisdom that a multitude of unenforced statutes of the law leads to a disrespect

of the law by the public, and that is one of the gun problems we have in Canada today.
It is my understanding that directives need only be sent to Crown prosecutors across Canada informing them that people found in possession of a weapon while having committed an offence should also be charged under either sectons 83, 84 or 86 of the present Criminal Code. Whether the sentence is served consecutively or concurrently will be left to the discretion of the judge. That is under the present law. If this does not work, then an amendment need only be made to those sections making the sentence mandatory.
One can only assume, from the lax and tolerant attitude of our present government to the present Criminal Code and from its past practice of not enforcing the laws therein, that any new legislation will be treated in the same manner, because during this debate over and over again we have heard that this bill will make law breakers out of many present law abiding citizens.
There are some points made in the paper submitted by the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police on gun control laws which I think are worthy of consideration during my participation in this debate. They point out that any improper type of legislation may cause more harm than good by imposing unnecessary restrictions on society. Years and years ago during the war I was told never to write a law that I was not prepared to enforce because, if I did so, I would have trouble on my hands. This is the best wisdom I was ever given, and I have carried it right through my life.
This paper lists three categories with which firearms are more and more frequently identified. The first is the sociopolitical movement which cannot be disregarded, and which historically has been associated with the manifestation of anti-establishment thinking that has accompanied the short or long drawn out process of government change. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, this is a major concern to many people in Canada today no matter what the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) says.
The second category deals with an element of society which will always choose to live off the avails of normal appetites but in a carrion fashion, with minimum personal effort and with total disregard of its effects toward society. This is the category of "crime for profit."
Then we come to the third category which is the crime passionel, that crime of violence which is committed in a moment of passion or temporary insanity.
The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police in their paper on gun control point out that in any of these categories those dedicated to crime will not or cannot submit to any law, and already disregard existing legislation. I agree with this statement and analogy. The problem at hand is the high incidence of crime and the search for methods to reduce it. If this can be achieved by the elimination of a weapon, then so much the better, but this approach can be discarded from the very beginning because violent crime can be committed with any number of weapons.
The Association of Chiefs of Police also say that "the causes of crime must be sought elsewhere-in the greed, hatred, jealousy and general moral depravity-and the remedy, if there be any, is more likely to be found in
April 12, 1976

morals and education, in improved police methods of detection", and I should like to add, in improved police methods of prevention. They conclude with the statement that "the prompt and certain imposition of punishment" is absolutely necessary. That is another thing we are not getting in Canadian society today.
I note with some astonishment that in both of these trade-off companion bills, C-83 and C-84, after years of the swinging door syndrome and permissive experiments in rehabilitation, we are now to enter an era of longer sentences. I ask: are our correction institutions now to become "vegetable farms"?
In this debate on principle where do we get a chance to review the very tragic and sad state of policy and management in our detention facilities?
The correctional services budget in 1960 was $19 million to $20 million, with a headquarters' staff of 50 people supervising a total penitentiaries' staff of 3,000 in Canada, overseeing over 6,000 inmates. The correctional services budget for 1975, according to the Blue Book, is over $230 million with a headquarters' staff and regional headquarters' staff of 620 people supervising a total penitentiaries staff in Canada of 7,000 people, looking after 8,800 inmates.
The measure of success in penal reform is the recidivism rate. In spite of the prolific growth in staff from 3,050 to 7,620 in 15 years, and in spite of the 1,100 per cent increase in expenditures in this service, the recidivism rate is still constant. Of all persons admitted to the penitentiaries in one year, about 80 per cent have had previous penal institutional experience, and 42 per cent to 45 per cent have had previous penitentiary experience. Where are the separate training facilities that are absolutely necessary if we are to start having proper rehabilitation measures in this area of first offenders? It is in this area that emphasis should be placed on rehabilitation programs.
I believe that for the objects stated by the Minister of Justice to be achieved, a rearrangement of priorities within this bill is needed. A separation of the gun control subject matter in this bill from the other aspects pertaining to peace and security would give this Thirtieth Parliament a chance to work up very meaningful legislation in this very important area of community need. When a government plays shallow political games with a subject as important as that covered by this bill, I guess it has no option but to hide its shame behind closure. I urge all members to support the important amendment of my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject with which Bill C-83 deals, the protection of society against crime, especially
Measures Against Crime
violent crime, is of paramount importance. The measures set out in the bill are part of a complex of measures the government has in mind for strengthening our criminal justice system. I believe, as one of the last speakers on the government side, that it is necessary to clarify a number of apparent misunderstandings about the measures we are putting forward.
The rationale for this bill, and for the other measures the government intends to introduce, is the need for a strong but reasoned response to the threat to our society posed by a pattern of constantly rising crime, in particular crimes of violence. There can be little doubt of the need for such a response. Between the first quarters of 1974 and 1975, for example, the incidence of robbery involving the use of firearms rose a staggering 74 per cent. Firearms are now used in 50 per cent of all murders; this proportion has been steadily increasing since the 1960's and is still growing. It is apparent that, to maintain and improve control of the situation, new initiatives such as those contained in the bill brought forward by the government are required.
The measures we are proposing in Bill C-83 are comprehensive. They affect dangerous offenders, special crime inquiries, changes in parole, changes in the penitentiaries and reformatories acts, protection of privacy, and measures to regulate firearms. These measures will receive searching examination in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and constructive commentary from the many organizations that have studied our measures. Both the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) will welcome their constructive submissions and suggestions. Before these measures are referred to that forum. Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a number of concerns that members raised in debate or that arose elsewhere.
I begin, Mr. Speaker, by reminding members who criticized the bill for being too comprehensive and including too many subjects that the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1969 and the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1975-76, Bill C-71, were also omnibus bills providing amendments to many different sections of the Criminal Code. Bill C-71, as members may remember, dealt among other matters with, drinking and driving, conspiracy, laundering money, protection of foreign diplomats, and cattle rustling. Omnibus bills of amendments provide a convenient and wholly appropriate method of keeping our laws relevant and consistent with changes in society, a method which this House has found acceptable before now.
Some members argue that Bill C-83 leaves too much to regulations and does not include sufficient legislative detail. It should be apparent that we cannot have bills both ways, both simple and complex at the same time. We believe Bill C-83 strikes the proper balance between statute and regulation, and that the regulations provided for in Bill C-83 are useful and necessary for lending flexibility to the implementation of some of the new measures put forward in the bill.
Other hon. members criticized the bill for omitting specific measures to deal with the hard drug problem and other causes of crime in this country. I fully agree with those hon. members; these are problems with which a minister of justice should be concerned and I trust that in the not too distant future the government will present the

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
House with the fruits of its long consideration of these matters. Meanwhile I call the attention of those hon. members to the fact that specific measures of the bill, such as the special sentencing provisions for the use of guns in the course of crime, and the strengthening of police powers with respect to electronic surveillance designed to strike more effectively at the crime bosses who control hard drug trafficking, are intended to attack the manifestations of some of the problems they raised.
As these and other measures demonstrate, the basic aim of Bill C-83 is to maintain control in the face of rising violence in our society, to help to restore to Canadians a sense of security and safety while preserving a delicate balance in the scales of justice between society's right to security and the rights of the individual. Let me now turn to its specific measures, Mr. Speaker, with a view to clarifying some of the misunderstandings that have arisen over the last ten days.
There were those, for example, who mistakenly criticized the government for introducing measures to register all rifles and shotguns, and those who attacked the bill for being ineffective in taking firearms away from criminals. Let me remind those members that two thirds of the murders in Canada take place between friends and acquaintances, not in the commission of other criminal acts, and that two thirds of the murders in Canada involving firearms are committed with rifles and shotguns. These facts demonstrate very clearly that there is a basic and overwhelming need for legislation in the area of firearms control such as we are proposing.
The government believes that the measures for the control of firearms contained in Bill C-83 will go a long way toward reducing gun related violence in Canada. They are an inter-connected and interdependent package that, taken together, as a whole, will grapple successfully, we think, with the major issues of misuse and abuse of firearms in Canada.
First, there is a licensing system, not for the weapons themselves, but for owners, a system in which all who want to own a rifle or shotgun will be required to demonstrate their fitness to own one. In adopting this measure the government rejected harsh solutions, such as a total ban on all weapons, the setting up of repositories where guns would be locked up when not in use, and registration of every rifle and shotgun. These were rejected because the costs outweighed any expected benefits and because, in the case of the first option, the government recognized that there are legitimate reasons for gun ownership, such as target shooting, hunting for sport or food, or for the joys of collectorship. As gun users themselves have pointed out, it is the person who kills, the gun is only the instrument.
What the government is proposing, Mr. Speaker, is no more and no less than the measures already in effect in respect to other dangerous instruments, whose possession is nevertheless legitimate and even necessary, such as automobiles. The government proposes simply to require individuals who wish to purchase or use firearms or ammunition to obtain a licence first, like an automobile driver. One licence, valid for five years, will cover any

number of rifles and shotguns, and any amount of ammunition. The sole test is fitness to possess a weapon.
Firearms will continue to be available to all responsible persons for all legitimate purposes, but persons with a history of violent behaviour or drug of alcohol abuse will be screened out. Surely members cannot object to that. Surely members cannot, as the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) stated the other day, endorse the present system whereby someone just released from prison or a mental hospital, or an individual in a sudden burst of emotion, can just walk into a store and buy a high powered rifle or shotgun, no questions asked.
That is one set of provisions of this bill, Mr. Speaker. The bill also contains stiffer penalties for criminals using guns while committing any indictable crime. Such a criminal will receive a mandatory, consecutive sentence ranging from one to 14 years in addition to any other penalty he may receive. Furthermore, he may be prohibited, by court order, from carrying or having in his possession any firearms or ammunition for any period of time specified.
As a further measure to deal with gun-related violence, Bill C-83 also provides greater police powers to search and seize firearms of all types wherever it is apparent that a crime is about to be committed, or that a person with a gun is a danger to himself and to others. This provision is primarily aimed at what the law euphemistically calls domestic quarrels.
We should bear in mind that two thirds of all murders in Canada arise from these household spats. They are the greatest source of danger to a police officer in the course of his or her duties. Common sense alone would seem to dictate that if a police officer is required to intervene, then that officer should be empowered to impound any weapon that presents a danger.
Finally, Bill C-83 tightens restrictions on importing and manufacturing weapons, adding Saturday night specials, sawed off rifles and shotguns, and all fully automatic weapons to the list of weapons forbidden in Canada. The bill also requires permits issued by the office of the Commissioner of the RCMP for the manufacture, wholesaling, and importing of firearms.
These then are the main provisions of our approach to the gun problem, a comprehensive approach including tighter regulations on private use to encourage private responsibility, more power to police to stop potentially dangerous situations before they develop, and the use of special additional prison sentences as a deterrent against armed crime.
In the near future, as a further measure, the government plans to complement the provisions restricting the general availability of guns by introducing across Canada a voluntary "turn-in-your-weapon program". There are more than ten million guns estimated to be in circulation in Canada at the moment. Although we rarely admit the fact, we have one of the highest per capita gun populations of any country in the world. Many of these weapons are not being used. Many are in all probability improperly stored in a closet or garage and represent a hazard. Brampton, Ottawa-the tragic shootings there prompted citizens to turn in their weapons by the hundreds. We are hoping to
April 12, 1976

persuade many other Canadians to do the same, and so lessen the potential for such tragedies in other localities.
During the debate some hon. members called attention to the fact that Bill C-83 contains no provision for mandatory testing or safety courses. In considering the question of firearms handling competence, one should be clear that while fitness to own a weapon is no guarantee that it will be properly handled, competence in its use-even a high degree of competence-is no guarantee of fitness. However, the bill does recognize the importance of considering firearms handling competence, and authorizes the Solicitor General to enter into agreements with the provinces to co-ordinate the administration of our provisions with their programs encouraging hunting and firearms safety training. We hope to include competency tests through this arrangement and, as the bill moves through the standing committee, the minister will be interested in hearing representations and further suggestions on this point.
Another hon. member raised the somewhat technical question of vicarious criminal liability. In other words, if someone steals your gun and shoots someone, could you be charged with murder? This is a question also raised by responsible hunting associations like the Canadian Wildlife Federation which, I should point out after some of the references this afternoon, endorses some of the proposals in Bill C-83, such as the ban on automatic weapons and increased police powers to seize firearms in the interests of safety. The answer to the question is, no. If there is any doubt implied in the wording of the bill, I am certain we shall want to correct this in committee.
What Bill C-83 does in this regard is to make you liable to be charged with careless handling and storage if it could be shown that the weapon was carelessly stored and that reasonable precautions for the safety of others had not been taken. Someone, for example, who leaves a loaded rifle on the front porch could be convicted and, if so, become liable to a penalty ranging from a suspended sentence to five years. The actual definition of carelessness will be for the courts to decide in each case. The courts have been required for a long time to assess carelessness, careless driving, for example, and should have no difficulty adjusting to this requirement.
Other comments pinpointed some necessary areas of revision in the bill; questions of minors' rights to shoot, the definition of ammunition, the provisions regarding gun collectors, and the effect of the bill on certain native groups. In the light of members' and others' comments and representations, the government is considering amendments in these areas and these will be pursued in committee.
Other measures in Bill C-83 include reforms of the detention system, about which the Solicitor General has already spoken, and measures concerning special crime inquiries, dangerous offenders and protection of privacy. With regard to special crime inquiries, I should like to say we are still reviewing the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Di Iorio case which upheld the rights of provinces to hold inquiries into organized crime. We will be re-examining the provisions of Bill C-83 in the light of that decision and the Minister of Justice will have more to say on this during the committee hearings.
Measures Against Crime
I should like to point out, while on the subject of crime inquiries, that our only interest here is to ensure that provincial governments have the adequate constitutional authority to proceed with those inquiries. As the bill indicates, our primary concern is to ensure that such investigation can be carried to completion. That is why our initial proposals give to the inquiring authority greater powers than a provincial authority could confer. As for the dangerous offenders sections of the bill, hon. members are aware that these provisions reflect the considered judgment of two committees, as expressed in the report of the Canadian Committee on Correction, known as the Ouimet report in 1969, and the Senate report on parole in Canada in 1974.
Both reports recommended changes in the criminal law so that criminals whose records of crimes of violence mark them out as constituting a serious and continuing threat to the physical safety of other people could be separated from society on a long-term basis. Indeterminate sentencing for offences of this kind is widely used in many countries whose penal practice is recognized around the world as progressive and enlightened. It provides an appropriate mechanism to protect society against dangerous criminals where it is virtually impossible at the point of sentencing to determine an appropriate length of sentence. The advantage of the indeterminate sentence lies in the fact that it postpones the decision on a release date to the point where authorities can more accurately judge the readiness of the dangerous offender to resume a normal life in the community without constituting a continuing threat to the safety and well-being of others.
Because of the gravity of this type of sentencing, the government has been careful to surround the provision with safeguards for the offender. The application for a sentence of indeterminate detention may be made by the Crown attorney only with the consent of the provincial attorney general. The offender can call any relevant evidence, including that of a psychiatrist, psychologist, or criminologist. The court may seek additional evidence by remanding the offender for medical observation for a limited period. Further, the indeterminate sentence must be reviewed within three years of the sentence, and every two years thereafter, by the National Parole Board.
I come now to the provisions that relate to the use of electronic surveillance. These provisions have raised concern on both sides of the House as to whether the bill strikes a proper balance between the need to provide effective protection for society and the need to safeguard the rights of the individual. The need for changes in this law to enhance our capability to attack the carefully protected bosses of organized crime in particular is evident, not least from the Solicitor General's report of 1975. In that report the Solicitor General explained that many of those convicted in the Quebec meat scandal might be free today if the present law had been in effect when the inquiry began.
The Minister of Justice also has the responsibility of protecting and upholding civil liberties in Canada, and he has welcomed the comments of civil liberties associations and other responsible groups and observers concerned with this area. The minister will wish to listen carefully to their proposals for change, notwithstanding that Bill C-83 pres-

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
ently includes a number of safeguards protecting civil liberties.
The changes in the Protection of Privacy Act that are proposed leave in place the already existing powerful guarantees against abuse of electronic surveillance. Judicial authorization continues to be a requirement. Unauthorized communications are themselves inadmissible in evidence. The act of illegal eavesdropping is punishable as a criminal offence. Full and free reporting of proceedings in open court is expressly permitted, thus ensuring the public right to keep fully informed of the way prosecutions are conducted and the way these investigative measures are being used. While we must ensure that the safeguards are adequate, we must not prevent our police forces from using the latest available technology in the fight against organized crime. Quite clearly, as long as the fundamental guarantees remain in place, the danger to the citizen is greater if we tie our hands needlessly in the fight against organized crime.
I should like to point out to hon. members that the proposed amendments carry the unanimous support of the provincial attorneys general who daily face the task of fighting criminals.
Admission of evidence derived from an unlawful surveillance is a similar problem, and its solution requires a similar perspective, Mr. Speaker. By deciding to admit such evidence and by repealing the suppression doctrine we have had in force, we are bringing wire tap laws into line with existing law on search warrants and more closely into line with our traditions of the common law. Some have argued that the measure rewards illegal conduct. In fact this is a narrow view of the issues involved.
As Wigmore, the great American authority on evidence, has noted, the exclusionary rule makes justice inefficient and coddles criminals by serving neither to protect potential victims nor to punish the offending officer. Rather, it punishes society by the release of criminals into our midst. Obviously, the solution to dealing with a case in which believable evidence has been illegally obtained by means of an unlawful wiretap lies in applying the existing legal sanctions rather than excluding the evidence. That is the balance that best protects the public and individual alike.
The measures contained in Bill C-83 comprise an over-all approach and they are part of a series of changes the government intends to introduce in the criminal justice system. Some commentators have mistakenly suggested that the proposals in the bill violate the spirit of the Law Reform Commission's recommendations. It is true that there are some specific items in the bill which differ from certain specific proposals of the commission, but the basic intent of our proposals is consistent with the commission's analysis of the underlying purpose of our common law. Indeed the latest report of the commission, which deals with this very subject, provides sound philosophical underpinning for that legislation.
Members of the House, particularly those who are also members of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, may recall the remarks of the former head of the Law Reform Commission, Mr. Justice Patrick Hartt-

Mr. Speaker, I have been looking forward to this debate on Bill C-83, but I have to ask myself right at the outset whether or not this is really a debate. Webster's dictionary says that to debate a subject is to discuss it by considering the opposing arguments, so it could hardly be called debate when the government has already made up its mind what it is going to do about the proposals in this bill.
The irony of this so-called debate is compounded by the government's determination to limit discussion on this extremely important and far-reaching legislation by bringing in closure, thereby disallowing the rights of many members to air their views. As you know, Mr. Speakers, the bill before us complicates the issue even further by dealing with so many different facets of crime, such as wiretap proposals, parole, prison breaks, changes in sentencing provisions, and other matters, some of which may have merit if they were dealt with on an individual basis. Instead we see them pooled together in an obvious effort to hide the inadequacies which exist in some of the individual proposals.
Because of the time restriction I will dwell on the one aspect of this bill that seems to be the prime concern of Canadians from coast to coast, and certainly a big concern of constituents in my riding, and that is the specific subject of the proposed firearms restrictions, registrations, and regulations, more commonly known as gun controls. We have seen clearly that the government is as totally disinterested in the weight of public opposition to the gun registration proposals in this bill as it is to capital punishment and other important issues.
I believe that it would be safe to say that every member of this House, including every member on the government benches, has received a great volume of mail on the subject of gun registration. I believe that it would be equally safe to say that the mail received by every single member has been overwhelmingly against the gun control provisions in this bill as they are written.

To continue my speech, Mr. Speaker, that is not to say that the Canadian people are against gun registration of any kind, or that they are against control of the sale, use and storage of weapons. More than anything else, it means that the Canadian people are completely fed up with the manner in which the government attempts to legislate. In practically every instance when the government tables legislation to deal with a real or imagined problem, it resorts to over-kill. There is no doubt whatever, Mr. Speaker, that the gun control section in this bill is over-kill, pure and simple.
Let me make it clear at the outset that as an individual who is horrified at the continuing increase of crime around us while the government allows known killers to walk our streets only to kill again, I would more than welcome and certainly support any legislation which would attempt to deal with the problems of law and order which we are faced with on a daily basis. Unfortunately, I see no way in which this bill as it now reads will effect a reduction in crime, particularly that part which pertains to gun control.
I was interested in the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), in respect of the government's contention that registered guns will not be used to kill people. I cannot draw any other conclusion from the statements of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Bas-ford) that we can curtail deaths in Canada caused by long guns by the simple expedient of registering the owners of rifles and shotguns. So many analogies have been used to illustrate the fallacy of such an argument that I will not relate them all here. However, I would like to bring to your attention the fact that a high percentage of homocides in this country are committed by handguns, which have been controlled for 50 years.
In all of the cases of long guns referred to by the government supporters of this legislation, every one of the persons involved in the deaths would have qualified for

registration certificates for the guns. Yet the government has the gall to include in this hodge podge legislation a type of gun control proposal that is only known to the deteriorating police states around the world. Let us not be so naive as not to realize that if a gangster is determined to commit a crime he will not need to register his firearm but rather obtain it through other devious ways and means which will exist even if these gun control proposals do become law.
Just think of the cost of administrating these controls on law abiding citizens. It will become a bureaucratic nightmare in more ways than one.
It would be ludicrous to suggest that any bureaucrat reviewing applications for gun registration could look into the future and, on the basis of what might happen, reject an application from an otherwise stable and law-abiding citizen. I will suggest to the hon. members of this House, though, that if we place too much authority in the hands of appointed bureaucrats to decide who can or cannot own a gun, it is going to lead almost automatically to abuse and, more than that, it is going to encourage the government, and its appointed bureaucrats, to extend this type of authority into other areas of lawful activity of Canadian citizens.
I would not pretend that I know more about what life is like in a controlled society, Mr. Speaker, but I at least know what it is like from personal experience. I know how easy it is for people in a society to accept the view that what a government is doing to them is for their own good. That is the way it happens. A government that is determined to assume control over a society that has known freedom will always adopt the manner of the great protector. "What we are doing is really for your own good, and it would be in your best interests to accept a certain amount of control in order to obtain long term benefits", it will say. Such governments are always the champions of human rights, civil rights, and all of the other rights that they plan eventually to curtail. That is what I fear the most from the government's assumption of control over our lives, Mr. Speaker.
The government pretends that it is doing all sorts of things for our own good, and I know where it can all lead. I have seen it happen. In view of the millions of people who are still living in the controlled society that I was able to escape from, I have to consider that I am one of the fortunate few. But I believed, as did millions of others, that I was comming to a country that offered a free society, freedom of all the things that communist countries in other parts of the world now control, and in fact that is what Canada has always been, a country exemplifying freedom to the rest of the world.
But what do we have today? We have a government in this country that wants the control over the means of production, over the ecomony, and over all aspects of human activity and endeavor. Like the governments in Eastern Europe its members are self-styled champions of civil liberty, individual freedom, and a wide range of human rights. It does not matter that these two philosophies are in conflit. It is what you can get the public to accept, and not necessarily what is right, that forms the basis of a philosophy that seeks to control people and societies. And that is precisely the type of society that the

If you reflect on how many of the above points are already in effect in this country you must begin to wonder just how much longer our democratic way of life will continue.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, the real key to what the government is attempting to do is its insistence that gun-related crimes can be controlled or curtailed by forcing law-abiding citizens to register as gun owners. It has been suggested a number of times by some of my colleagues in these debates that the logical next step is to register all owners of baseball bats, kitchen knives, hatchets and axes, and all other instruments and objects that are used to commit violent crimes.
The fact of the matter is as the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) pointed out, that we cannot outlaw the instruments of death any more than we can outlaw death itself. Lethal weapons as such are already controlled as well as they can be controlled by being included as offences in the Criminal Code. Sawed-off rifles and shotguns, automatic weapons, and revolvers are already classed as either restricted or prohibited weapons in the Criminal Code, yet most gun-related crimes in Canada, as in other countries, are committed with restricted or prohibited weapons.

The logical way to tighten up the law is to tighten the laws that are being abridged by criminals. Adding still more weapons to the restricted classes is not going to prevent or curtail gun-related crime. Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe the Minister of Justice is as naive as this gun-control legislation makes him out to be, so I have to suspect that there is a more sinister motive behind it, one that has nothing whatever to do with controlling crime.
I know as well as any other person in Canada that the government is bankrupt of ideas when it comes to getting violent crime under control, and I know that neither the Minister of Justice nor the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) is all that concerned about the problem. How could a minister be concerned about controlling crime when he states publicly, before any legislation is even tabled, that he will not be a party to the execution of a person convicted of a brutal, vicious and deliberate murder? How can we believe that such a minister would follow up and ensure that such a murderer would really be kept in prison for twenty-five years? The answer is simple. We can't.
Allow me to point out that there are many other individuals and groups of individuals who share this view publicly. For example, just last Friday the committee representing the rank and file of the RCMP from across Canada expressed their concern that their boss, the Solicitor General, was "unable to be effective as the federal minister responsible for the force." Is there any wonder? They are talking about the same minister who just a few weeks ago said that Soviet KGB secret agents aren't spies. Perhaps he believes they are butchers, bakers or candlestick makers-or even diplomats.
In any case how can we trust a government to protect society when, for example, convicted rape murderers of children are allowed out of prison on daily and weekend passes, to commit further crimes? How can we trust this government to control convicted criminals when almost every week we see another prison break, or another taking of hostages by hardened prisoners? The obvious answer, again, is that we simply can't. We can only trust the government to chip away at the rights and freedoms of the law-abiding citizens.
The Minister of Justice insists that capital punishment is not a deterrent to violent crime, and says that the answer is to impose longer prison terms for certain types of murder. I'm glad that the minister can at least distinguish between the various types of murder. No doubt when this legislation is railroaded through the House we will have two more types of murder-murders committed with registered guns, and murders committed with unregistered guns.
The plain fact is that the minister does not know whether or not the threat of execution would be a deterrent to certain types of premeditated murder. We don't have any data on which to base such an assumption for the simple reason that the cabinet in the past ten years has commuted every death sentence imposed by our courts, therefore breaking the very laws which it passed. Parliament compromised on the contentious issue of capital punishment and voted to impose the death sentence for conviction of the murder of a policeman or prison guard. While we don't have any data on the deterrent effect of the death penalty we do have records that show that some of those murderers

whose sentences have been commuted by the Liberal cabinet have gone on to commit further crimes, including murders.
I am afraid that we are going to find ourselves in the same position that the people of California, and other states, now find themselves in as a result of the U.S. Supreme court decision banning capital punishment. That infamous murdering animal, Charles Manson, who had his death sentence commuted to life imprisonment after being convicted in 1969 for seven senseless murders, will be eligible for parole in 1978, just two years from now. Just think of it?
It is a mockery of justice and a sad commentary on any society to allow such a situation to exist. It is not a situation that exists only in the United States or in other countries remote from us. We have our own Charles Man-sons, whether we want to accept that fact or not, and I do not want to turn such people out on leave, parole or full release, to prey again and again on innocent people, until at least they are cornered, and either shot down by the police or returned to a jail cell for a few more years. Unless we are prepared at least to put the death penalty to the test, and find out once and for all if it will deter violent and senseless murders, then we are not doing all we can do, and all we should do, to protect the innocent and law-abiding.
The Minister of Justice said a few days ago that this gun registration legislation will keep guns out of the hands of the irresponsible. What complete and utter nonsense! The irresonsible in society acquire guns in the same irresponsible way that they do everything else. The minister is insulting our intelligence when he suggests we can control the actions of the lawless by imposing new restrictions on the actions of the law-abiding people of Canada.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that people are not against some control over the sale, storage or use of firearms. No sensible person would agree that firearms should be immediately available to all sorts of people, in stores, by mail order, or by simply picking up a rifle or shotgun that is left lying around by its owner. I repeat that the Minister of Justice is resorting to overkill, instead of studying the matter thoroughly and sensibly.
The minister should be attacking the weak points in our gun laws, not the strong points. Gun clubs and other organizations concerned with the safe and responsible handling of guns are not the weak points in the gun question. These are the groups who would be in the strongest position with respect to limiting the irresponsible distribution, storage and use of firearms. These are the people who have pioneered the safe use of firearms, and who have carried the burden of education and instruction in the safe use of firearms. It is these people who have brought pressure to bear on the provinces, in the absence of any federal programs, to introduce gun safety courses.
In Ontario, for example, we have an excellent program of gun safety and hunter safety. No person in Ontario can buy a hunting license without first completing a hunter safety course and passing both a written and practical examination. The graduate receives a certificate which is presented to the agency selling hunting licences. It is a serious offence for anyone to sell a hunting licence without verifying that the buyer has such a certificate.

However, the problem here, is that the Minister of Justice simply doesn't seem to be able to come up with any concrete proposals for dealing with violent crime. His sympathies seem to be more with the rights and dignities of those convicted of crimes, and so his tendency is to vent his frustration on the innocent victims of crime and the law-abiding citizens of Canada. He can't bring himself to the point of allowing the state to take the life of a convicted murderer, and he can't seem to find any way of deterring those who follow a deliberate and calculated life of crime, especially those who use guns in the commission of crimes. And so, Mr. Speaker, the minister has decided to kill all the chickens in order to foil the fox. Of course this is a cop-out, but that is not new or unique to this government. It is a form of deceit, something at which the government is adept.
The minister says gun registration as proposed in this legislation is not intended to be confiscation. He says that in place of the death penalty we will impose longer, mandatory prison sentences. He promises a lot of things, Mr. Speaker, but we just cannot believe him. I think back on the multi-million-dollar campaign waged by the Prime Minister in 1974 against the wage and income control program advocated by the former leader of the opposition. The Prime Minister convinced the people of Canada that such a program would not work. And after his government was returned to majority power he imposed the present wage and price control program on the country, a program which had already been worked out in principle at the very time he was attacking our own program.
I cannot accept this bill on any count, Mr. Speaker, neither the gun control proposals, the wiretap proposals, the changes in sentencing provisions in the Criminal Code! the changes with respect to dangerous offenders, parole, nor the proposals for dealing with prison breaks. My objections have already been very ably defined in the remarks of my Conservative colleagues during this limited so-called debate. The fact remains that the government continues to shy away from including any specific details of law in any of the bills it has tabled in recent years.
I am suspicious of any open-ended legislation where the details are filled in after the bill has been passed by parliament. We should be voting on specific details rather than broad principles, and in the case of gun registration in particular I want to know what sort of bureaucracy the government plans to install to administer the law. I want to know exactly what regulations and conditions a person will have to contend with when he or she enters a registration office to apply for a gun registration certificate. It is not unreasonable for members of this House to want to know what they are voting for or against.
That is the reason why all these very important crime issues cannot and must not be pooled in a single misleading piece of legislation such as the one before us. It is easy to see that this devious Liberal government is continuing to try to fool the public. In this case it is most obviously trying to soften the people of Canada into believing that making this bill law, capital punishment will no longer be necessary. I think that the government has been fooling the people of Canada long enough, and I sincerely hope and believe that the public will not fall for it again.

The government has presented Bill C-83 for parliament's consideration and decision. This piece of legislation comes under the general heading of peace and security. When we start thinking about peace and security we tend to think of widening police authority, prohibiting certain acts or instruments, and toughening penalties.
Our children and, I suppose, we as adults get a lot of romantic ideas from American television programs such as police shows, where in every case we see the police making an arrest we see them warning the arrested person of his right to remain silent and if he should say anything it could be used later on in prosecuting him. We do not have that right in Canada. As a matter of fact I know that our police force has indeed very wide powers, much wider than in the country to the south of us. So if we get a romantic view from television and think that Canadians also have these rights which we see on U.S. television, then we should be informed that such is not the case.
Not so long ago I had occasion to write to the Attorney General of the province of Ontario about the case of a young man who was arrested in a hotel in Sudbury and taken to the local jail. What was his offence? He was suspected of smoking grass in the hotel. He demanded to make one phone call to his lawyer, which he thought he had the right to do, but the police promptly booted him to the jail and told him he had no such right and he would stay in jail until they should decide what they would do with him.
The widening of police powers is one of the things that concerns many people in this country. In the bill before us the government seems intent on impressing on the Canadian people that it is the last buffer of security against a rising tide of crime and violence. Therein lies my first criticism of Bill C-83. It includes six particular items, from entirely new legislation governing the ownership of long guns, to amending present legislation covering habitual offenders and dangerous sexual offenders, electronic surveillance, special crime inquiries and custody and release of inmates.

Of all the items in Bill C-83 gun control has attracted by far the greatest attention, and in some parts of the country more than others. In my riding of Nickel Belt, which is predominantly rural and working class, there is great concern about certain provisions, which concern has resulted in about 180 pieces of mail daily, plus a 6,000 signature petition. I understand the basic resentment of the people in my area against certain provisions of the bill. They see it basically as legislation aimed at large urban centres like Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa, where a firearm is not looked on in the same manner as in rural areas. Indeed many of the folk in my area say that this legislation is for those urban crazies who do not know about or have any respect for firearms and who want to shoot each other. They feel they are being put through this bureaucracy for the sake of protecting urban dwellers from each other.
In Nickel Belt most of the workers are employed in mines or smelters, and when work is finished, or on week ends, hunting and fishing are indispensable forms of relaxation. Many of the workers have hunt camps or cottages and spend time in the summer and fall hunting and fishing.
They are also concerned about the cost of any kind of licensing program. One constituent pointed out to me that he now pays $15 for a moose licence, $5 for a licence for hunting migratory birds, and $10 for a deer licence, and after those costs there is also the cost of a hunting licence. Now there is a proposed gun licence fee which is as yet undetermined. My constituents see this additional cost a further proof that eventually hunting will be reserved for the rich.
My constituents have also expressed concern about the engulfing red tape of bureaucracy. By nature, rural folk seem to be much more resentful about encroaching bureaucracy than urban folk, probably because they are much more self reliant. In particular, they are set against the proposal to have two guarantors testifying as to the character of a prospective gun owner.
Concern has been expressed about the provision of search and seizure without warrant. In particular, if no charge has been laid, the firearm owner ought to be able to claim his property unless the licensing action is in progress or some charge has been laid.
Another question raised by my constituents deals with reimbursement. If, during the initial three year licensing period, a person is not issued a licence to own a firearm and the registrar issues an order to take his property, will that person be reimbursed? That is very important to the people in my constituency. I have met with members of rod and gun clubs and other interested citizens and listened to their opinions, and expressed mine, in the hope that this legislation can be as effective as possible.
I support the principle of gun control. Indeed the bill does not go far enough with respect to tightening gun control. I have said this to rod and gun clubs and those interested in my constituency, and there are large numbers of them.

However, the area in which I think this legislation will make some difference is in the inter-familial relationship or with regard to the person who is mentally unbalanced, either long range or temporarily, the person who is a violent alcoholic or who has had a criminal record, who is out on probation or who is out on bail awaiting trial. I think these classes of people ought not to be permitted to have the responsibility of bearing a firearm, and that is where I see this legislation being effective. I have taken that position in my constituency. It is not a very popular position, but in conscience I could take no other. I reject the argument put forward by hon. members in this House, and also by people at large, that it is a right to have a firearm. I must confess that I know of no such right.
I think this matter has less to do with rights and more to do with maturity. It seems to me that it is a privilege to own a firearm, and it is certainly the responsibility of the state to determine who can legally bear firearms and under what conditions. The same attitude should prevail with regard to drivers' licences. It is not a right of a citizen to have a driver's licence, it is a responsibility, and I think too often in the past we have been stressing our rights more than we have been stressing our responsibilities. This is an area in which we have been far too lax in the past.

When there were such unfortunate and tragic incidents as those in Brampton and in Ottawa, my office received letters from southern Ontario and from everywhere else asking why we parliamentarians were not doing something about tightening up gun control. It seemed that everything died down three or four weeks after that. Now we are getting the other backlash that people do not want controls.
It is easy to see in respect of this kind of situation, this easy access to firearms, that we are playing Russian roulette, with innocent people at the end of the barrel. This concerns me as a parliamentarian and as someone who must look at this bill and make a decision on it. Unfortunately the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) are not in the House this evening. However, I want to say to them that the gun control section must be further tightened.
I, and many of my constituents, believe that the guarantor provision should be dropped because it will not be effective. This provision is not the same as that in respect of the guarantor of a passport. A guarantor of a passport is one who, for example, certifies that he has known the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) for two years and can state that the picture submitted is a reasonable facsimile of him. That is not the same as the provision in this bill. We are not asking for identification. We are asking the guarantor, under the provision in this bill, to make an assessment of the character of the applicant and to state whether or not he is a person of character who could be entrusted with a firearm. It seems to me that is entirely different.
Even in rural communities where everyone knows everyone else there would be a difficulty in getting someone to be a guarantor for a person to be permitted to obtain a licence. It seems to me that in an urban situation, such as Toronto, no one ever gets to know anyone else. Therefore I do not see how one could find two guarantors who would be prepared to say that one is a person of such a character that one should be permitted to be licenced.

For instance, the guarantor may be a school principal. This missed the whole point. Today the schools are very large composite schools. The principal never knows who the students are. It is the guidance cousellor who deals with the pupils. The principal is an administrator who, in an urban area, could never testify concerning the character of his students. It seems to me there is another arguments which we should keep in mind which I believe is valid in this connection. I refer to the argument that this will become an elitist thing. It seems to me that certain classes will be certifying certain other classes. The elitist class will be classified as the lawyer, the judge, the school principal, and so on.

speechtext: And a teacher.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
No; a school principal. It seems to me that this involves a certain class distinction. It provides, apart from that elitism, as I have said, no real safeguards. I and many of my constituents think that we should be moving to drop that provision in respect of a guarantor, and instead have the registrar of firearms as the official who would make the decision in every case on the basis of the facts so far as he is aware of them. For example, psychiatric hospitals which are treating dangerously mentally deficient persons and who are moving back and forth from the community to the hospital would pass this information on to the registrar. This information now is passed to the local police force but it could just as easily be passed to the registrar. He could also be furnished information concerning any persons who are out on parole, or who are out on bail, or who have been convicted of a crime in the past.
If these names were passed on to the registrar then, if such a person should apply for a licence, the registrar would institute a check and make a decision on the basis of the facts available to him. In addition I think it is very important that the competency test be included at this stage before any licence is issued. In other words, the person applying must conform not only to the requirement of not having a record which would prohibit his obtaining a licence but he should also provide a competency certificate, and on that basis he will or will not be given a licence. That competency certificate would indicate that he or she had successfully completed a course in gun handling. It seems to me that is a role gun clubs could play in teaching people the proper way to handle and the best way to care for and store a firearm.
I also believe that the registering of guns should be under the aegis of the government rather than contracted out to the private sector. This would avoid the all too prevalent pork-barreling which we see flourishing all too easily in this country these days. With regard to the licensing, I feel it ought not to exceed $5 for at least the first five year licensing period. At the end of the first five year period the situation could be reviewed. I feel also that in the matter of search and seizure of a firearm without warrant the citizen ought to get his firearm back unless a charge is laid under the Criminal Code, or unless for some reason his licence is being revoked.
In respect of the initial licensing period, if an individual cannot be licensed and the registrar causes his firearm to be confiscated then that person should be reimbursed for
April 12, 1976

his property. I would urge that the gun control section of Bill C-83 be amended along the lines I have noted.
However, there is a part of Bill C-83 which causes me great apprehension. I refer to the wiretapping provisions. During the minority parliament of 1972-74 parliament passed a bill which set up wiretap provisions. Now we have the spectacle of the government in a majority position wanting to put back into the wiretap legislation provisions which parliament had previously rejected. A speaker on the government side of the House argued that it is necessary to have electronic surveillance because that is how we could get at the top people-the dons of the mafiosi. I do not think he realizes that the top mafiosi today do not use the telephone. They are much smarter and wiser in that particular area. So I do not think any people of this type will be trapped in that way.
