speechtext: They use the Liberal committee rooms.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Well, I have known them to be used for other things. This particular part of Bill C83 dealing with electronic surveillance to me is most regressive. It seems to me that the state has not made its case for additional powers under the wiretap legislation of Canada. Indeed it gives more arbitrary power to the police without a corresponding protection for the individual citizens' privacy.
I have no experience in this matter so I must believe what other persons with experience and some expertise have said. Ramsey Clark, former United States attorney general and one with considerable experience, made the following points about such surveillance:
a.	wiretapping was not used between 1966 and 1969 yet indictments against members of organized crime tripled; he concluded that wiretapping is a wasteful and inefficient means of investigation and is not, moreover, effective against organized crime;
b.	wiretapping destroys the professionalism of investigators; electronic surveillance encourages not investigation, but just sitting waiting for something to happen;
c.	it is enormously expensive-for example, the use of laser beams which can pierce walls up to 12 feet thick;
d.	such all-encompassing eavesdropping evades human dignity-e.g. the listening in on the sexual activities of Martin Luther King and the subsequent use of this information to smear King's reputation.
On the face of it it would seem to me that these amendments, with respect to electronic surveillance, give the police a licence to invade the privacy of any or all citizens without any authorization. Who will prosecute the police?
The present law at least provides defence counsel with an opportunity to determine whether unlawful surveillance did take place. The requirement for notification to be given to the person who has undergone electronic surveillance at least provides citizens with protection against an over-zealous police force. The government argues this requirement has seriously inhibited electronic surveillance, because notification alerts the potential offender before the investigation can be completed. The example the government gives is that "such investigations can be of a long-term nature and sometimes unproductive periods of some length occur where, for example, the subject is out of the country". The government should be required to provide statistics. How often has this happened? The proposed amendment increases the potential period of surveillance
Measures Against Crime
from 60 days to 120 days. But as the government itself argues, 60 days is usually enough.
In 1975, under section 178.12 of the Criminal Code, 555 authorizations were granted, and 449 renewals were approved. Apparently only two renewals were refused. Considering the track record, it is difficult to see why section 178.23(2b) does not provide the police with enough leeway to complete investigations. Coupled with proposed authorization periods, this proposal gives them a minimum surveillance period of 210 days. The government should tell us how many requests under section 178.23(2b) have been made and how many refused, and also how many convictions resulted from electronic surveillance.
According to the government another difficulty concerning notification requirement is this: it has inhibited the investigation of organized crime. Actually fault did not lie with the notification requirement; it lay with the types of offences for which authorizations can be granted. For instance, the present law dictates that authorization for interception may only be granted in respect of certain, specific indictable offences and any indictable offence involving organized crime. I call on the Minister of Justice to revoke that particular section as, potentially, it offers no greater security to Canadians than the present law does; on the contrary, it could undermine confidence in the state.
Let me say a word about crime inquiries as provided for in the bill. I do not disagree with this provision, but merely raise one point. I want to see the innocent protected. Sometimes, when inquiries are in high gear, the innocent are dragged in. Too often, in the mind of the public the innocent are judged as guilty merely because they are involved in the investigation. It seems to me that the minister should draft provisions to ensure that such inquiries do not become witch hunts but, rather, protect the integrity of the innocent.
Let me now say a word about the dangerous offender section. I suggest that, at the time of review of the indeterminate sentence by the National Parole Board, the board should be expanded with the addition of two persons who should come from the community into which the offender says he wants to be released. In relation to the section dealing with custody and release of inmates, there is nothing there that I disagree with, in principle.
In summary, I cannot support the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). He wants to send the subject matter of the bill to committee because he knows that by so doing he would kill the bill. I want the bill to go to committee, witnesses to appear and, hopefully, constructive amendments to be moved. Hence I support the bill in principle and will exercise my prerogative on third reading, when I shall see the bill after it has been through the committee stage, and after I have once again consulted concerned groups in my riding.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we near the end of debate of second reading I wish to comment on areas of the bill which I hope will receive careful examination and possibly be amended in committee. This debate takes place at a time when people are concerned about the rise in crimes of violence and want protection. It is important to make sure that the measures we adopt are effective, realistic, and afford that protection. But it is also

April 12, 1976
Measures Against Crime
important not to put in place measures so repressive as to be antithetical to rehabilitation.
Let me speak on wiretapping. I sympathize with the police viewpoint, with their contention that they need additional powers to deal with organized crime. From my own experience in corrections, I would say that the majority of people incarcerated are socially incompetent minor criminals, while the so-called "master criminal" often goes free. I do not wish to see the police restricted in their very necessary investigative work, especially if they are to reverse this trend. However, I am concerned about electronic surveillance, even when done with a judge's warrant. I think wiretapping represents an intrusion into people's lives which should be monitored very carefully. Representing, as I do, an ethnic riding where people are sometimes handicapped by lack of knowledge of English, where dissimilar names often seem similar by reason of unfamiliarity, and where mistakes in identity are made, I am concerned about the possible complications in the life of an innocent person which could result from a police file being built up about him or her.
The present requirement that people be notified after a certain period if police surveillance does not lead to a charge is, I think, a doubtful safeguard. I can understand the view of the police, that it limits their investigation of criminals and may in fact serve as a warning to a wide criminal network to go underground temporarily. But from the viewpoint of the innocent person I think such notification after the event can cause much anxiety and distress and will not necessarily result in corrective action, namely, the destruction of the file. I therefore suggest that either the regulations or an amendment to this bill-and I prefer the latter-should stipulate that in the event of an investigation not leading to a criminal charge after a certain period, all records of the wiretapping should be destroyed. There ought to be a verification procedure, to show that the records have been destroyed.
Let me now talk about the dangerous offender. Bill C-83 contains "dangerous offender" provisions to replace the "habitual criminal" and "dangerous sexual offender" categories. This is in line with the Ouimet committee recommendations of 1969, and with similar recommendations of the Canadian Mental Health Association committee on legislation and psychiatric disorders brought forward in the same year. The "dangerous sexual offender" category has been badly used. Sometimes the result has been excessively long imprisonment for people whose patterns of behaviour, although socially and morally objectionable, were not dangerous.
It is important not to confuse sexual behaviour with aggressive behaviour. Exhibitionists and other sexual nuisances are sometimes seen as being launched on a progressive route to rape; but figures obtained both in the United States and Canada show that convicted rapists are much more likely to have previous convictions for violent offences like assault or break and enter than for exhibitionism, voyeurism, and so on. It is important to protect the community from dangerous offenders, but that will not be done by locking up the socially and sexually incompetent.

Methods of prediction of dangerousness have been improved and refined considerably in recent years, but the definition of "serious personal injury" in this bill merits very careful examination if indeed it is to encompass the truly dangerous.
Turning to the Parole Act, I am pleased to see the proposal to add to the parole board representatives of the community to which an inmate is returning, in some cases. This first-hand knowledge of local conditions and feeling, and the supports or stresses the parolee will encounter should improve the decision making.
I have some concern however, about the parole board assuming responsibility for granting all absences from institutions. It is true that unwise decisions on unescorted absences have been made by some institutional staff, but there is no guarantee that the parole board will make better decisions.
In a well-run institution, correctional staff should consider it part of their professional responsibility to know prisoners as individuals, to know whatever potential an individual prisoner has for constructive, socially useful behaviour, and to support acceptable goals in positive ways. In this context arranging temporary absence for useful purposes can be an important rehabilitative tool.
If correctional staff are not using it wisely, they should be assisted to develop their judgment and prediction skills. However, to take away from them the decision making and, therefore, the responsibility to think about the factors that enter into decisions is to risk a static custodial program without much dynamism or interest in change.
I note that there is provision for the National Parole Board to delegate the authority to grant temporary absence without escort, and I hope this will be used where appropriate. Bill C-83 suggests that the decision to delegate will be made on the basis of some inmate criteria. The wording is "an inmate or class of inmate". It will undoubtedly be useful to develop criteria of this kind, but the competence and skills of staff enter into this too and they tend to vary from one institution to another, depending on the leadership and quality of staff development.
With regard to remission, I am pleased to see statutory remission abolished as I think it was meaningless and confusing. However, to ensure that earned remission really is earned, that it provides positive incentives for inmates to involve themselves in constructive work or study, it will be important to ensure that there is a clear and well developed evaluation system so that the remission is not credited in an automatic way.
If remission is earned and well earned, I think it should be forfeited only in very grave circumstances. I would, therefore, like to see an amendment to the proposal in the bill which provides for forfeiture for "any disciplinary offence". If staff and inmates know that remission, once earned, will be forfeited only for grave reason, which could be defined, there is more likelihood that the inmate will try to earn it and that staff will award it carefully.
This bill essentially deals with violent crime and the prevention of it. It is urgent that public confidence be restored since people have been disquieted by the rise of violent crime. With gun controls in place and with public
April 12, 1976

confidence restored by the passage of this bill as amended, I trust, it will then be important to direct our attention to the prevention of crime. I think one needs to look at this in four steps.
Obviously everything we do in the way of social legislation-housing, income maintenance, family law, education and child welfare-is prevention of crime in the broadest sense. It is no accident that the inhabitants of our training schools, reformatories, and eventually penitentiaries, overwhelmingly come from disadvantaged families.
The second layer of prevention of crime comes in adequate policing. Here I refer not only to the community officer who can do a great deal to defuse situations where the ordinary law-abiding citizen might find himself in difficulty and who does a great deal of preventive work with youth, but also the visible uniformed policemen whose presence has been shown to cut down on certain kinds of crime, notably break and entry.
Third, I hope that we will soon be debating some of the important recommendations of the Law Reform Commission, particularly on sentencing. We have too many ineffectual relatively minor offenders in jails who would be better in community programs, leaving the prisons for the dangerous offender who needs to be out of circulation for a certain time. Measures to keep the offender in the community also provide opportunities to encourage accountability. The offender who is obliged to make reparation and remains in the community to make reparation is perhaps faced each day with the realization of what he or she has done in a way that the inmate in a prison is not.
There are many of the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission for innovative sentencing which could be implemented under present legislation. One must hope that attitudes of judges will change so that there is more interest in sentencing in ways that benefit the community and that reserve prison sentences for those where it really is essential.
For those who do get to institutions, it is important that there be a spectrum of institutions, from the community residence or hostel type right through to maximum security. The provisions in this bill for provincial-federal agreements are, I hope, the beginning of an attempt to use the facilities more wisely and more constructively.
Very often in a province such as Ontario you have three, four or five layers of institutions being run under provincial auspices, and the same under federal auspices. More sensible combined use would make it easier to get an individualized program for a person at a particular stage of his or her existence, and allow maximum security to be used not only as a holding place, bus as a place in which a person could be assisted to acquire greater control and move gradually on to a program more suited to whatever improvement he or she was showing.
Finally, I am pleased to see in this bill one amendment to the Prisons and Reformatories Act. I hope it is the beginning of many because the Prisons and Reformatories Act is a very outdated piece of legislation which badly needs many other improvements.
Measures Against Crime

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my contribution by paying tribute to the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) who gave us a very lucid and well thought out presentation on the subject, giving credit where credit was due, but pointing out the weaknesses in the bill.
I have often thought as I surveyed this measure that it was sponsored by the wrong minister when it was sponsored by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). Maybe it should have been sponsored by the Minister of Immigration, who is also responsible for Manpower (Mr. Andras); it coud have come under the job creation program since obviously it will require a great deal of manpower to administer.
I have in my hands a publication, dated March 9, which was sent to me and, I suppose, to all members, by the B.C. Wildlife Federation. In this document the executive of the federation says the Treasury Board has already approved 900 new positions just to start this program. Based on the fact that the government has just indicated there will be registrars or licence issuers established throughout Canada for the public's convenience, the federation estimates that the program will require in the order of between 10,000 and 15,000 new civil servants, meaning a bill in the area of between $200 and $300 million. To add a final touch to this picture, the government has already indicated that the licence holders will pay for the entire cost of the program. On the basis of the issuance of three million licences for gun-owners in Canada, the annual licence fee could conceivably be in the area of $100 a year. This is staggering in itself. It amazes me, though, that this bill should be called "peace and security legislation".
I realize, of course, that the people of Canada want security, but I am reminded of an old adage, "The people are asking for bread and are being given a stone." Everyone is in favour of peace; everyone is in favour of security. And the people who are hungry for it most will be those most disappointed by the legislation. If this legislation were intended to produce peace and security one would think it would focus on those who violate peace and security the most, and while the bill does give some credible attention to that aspect it is nevertheless true that the people who will be affected most are those who are already respectful of law and order. The part dealing with firearms affects hundred of thousands of people who already peace loving, while the sections dealing with criminals are in a very small minority.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. To support the point I am making I should like to quote an hon. member who is the chairman of the justice committee, the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), who pointed out that only three paragraphs are directed to crime prevention while the rest are "an inefficient tool to fight crime". That is a member on the government side speaking, and he is the chairman of the committee. I certainly support the proposal put forward by my hon. friend from Calgary North that the bill be split up into separate parts.
I might draw it to the attention of the House that the section on the crime commission is already anachronistic since the decision of the Supreme Court validating the operation of the crime commission in Quebec. Thus it would appear that some of the legislation is already out of date. I might add that this Supreme Court decision accepting the point that we are in a field of provincial jurisdiction would indicate that much of the bill before us ought possibly be referred to the Supreme Court for a decision as to its constitutionality.
It would seem to be a cardinal principle to follow that if we want good legislation we ought to consider the people who are affected most by it, as well as those who are knowledgeable regarding the subject. It came as a great surprise to me that the Department of the Solicitor General, while it did contact members of the public at large, notably members of the B.C. Wildlife Federation, did so well into the program, at which point the department did not even know that already in British Columbia there is a licensing program in existence which makes training and competence mandatory. When the officials of the federation offered their counsel and help, the offer was apparently turned down. I guess by this time it can be taken for granted that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) would turn down that kind of competent advice. This is why we so often find duplication in government services across Canada. The provinces already have a good program in operation and now the federal government wants to duplicate it.
It seems to me there are several important principles of law which ought to be followed in this legislation. The first is that the very existence of a law ought to act as a deterrent to wrongdoing. This is why speed limit signs are posted. It is not enough that the law be there; it has to be obvious, it has to be made evident so that the public knows where it's at. These gun control provisions are a deterrent only to those who already have a solid core of good will. For those who are bent on doing evil the existence of a law such as this will not be any deterrent at all. Therefore there has to be a deterrent in addition to the law, punishment for violating the law.
Second, the law, to operate properly, ought to encourage responsibility for behaviour. The hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) just pointed this out and I think she is entirely correct. One of the failures of our society is this: we have not taught people to accept responsibility for their behaviour. In most cases when young people are brought before the courts, the judge simply turns them over to their parents or to another agency, slaps their wrists and

says, "If you are good in future, everything will be all right." There is no thought of restitution, or at least, not often enough. Our people are not growing up with a sense of the need to be accountable for their behaviour.
One of the functions of law ought to be to make us responsible for what we do but, sad to say, much of the bail practice, much of the parole system, focuses not on being responsible but on finding ways of getting out of having to be responsible. I hate to say it, but some of my good friends in this Chamber who are lawyers have focused not on getting justice for their clients but on helping their clients to get off. That leads to a total miscarriage of justice. The focus ought to be upon providing justice for society; and the law should make us responsible for our behaviour.
Third, the law ought to be enforced uniformly. There ought to be equity in the disposition of the law. The problem I find with Bill C-83 is that it will be impossible to enforce the bill uniformly. For example, I have in my riding a competitive marksman who travels across Canada to compete. He has in his arsenal of handguns seven very finely tooled pistols. Under this legislation he cannot even travel across Canada to compete any more because he would violate the law.
It is easy to say that he can do it under the Olympic regulations, Mr. Speaker, but the Olympic regulations allow only two classifications, and this gun owner is an expert in seven. That is point No. 1. The second point is that if he is going to travel across Canada to compete he has to carry spare parts with him. This might be another pin, a clip-anything he needs in case one of his handguns breaks down. Under this legislation he would have to have another licence to carry those extra parts. It is impossible under this legislation to be equitable to all people.
Another class affected by the legislation is the antique dealer. In my riding there is a collector who has a mobile museum of guns. People come and see his museum all the time, and he travels around with it to show people. What is this man to do under the legislation? Various suggestions have been made in the House about making these guns inoperative by doing a little welding on them or disfiguring them in some way. But as soon as he makes his guns inoperative, their value as antiques is diminished. These guns are, in a sense, his life savings, his investment.
As other hon. members in this House have said, the gun legislation before us tends to make law breakers out of honest citizens. The people who are law abiding will conform with it. Those who do not have this hard core of good will in them will violate the law without compunction. The law abiding citizen will be hassled and harassed; the other person will not.
Then there are the violent in society, those who believe in violence and who live by violence. I have watched them operate. I have been on the streets where they have operated. Violence is a way of life to them. They believe that the establishment is wrong, that the establishment is corrupt, that it is a case of being more upright and moral by trying to overthrow the establishment than by being part of the establishment. It almost becomes a point of righteousness to help destroy the establishment with this kind of perverted morality.
April 12, 1976

What are we going to do about these people, Mr. Speaker? Are we going to give those with a distorted sense of morality the opportunity to escape the full force of this legislation? Are we going to take away the rights of the large mass of people who are already law-abiding and not deal with the violent in our society? As I have said, it is impossible to have uniform enforcement of this legislation.
Let me give the House an example. If you do not store your weapons properly, Mr. Speaker, you can be liable for up to five years' imprisonment for careless storage. But a person who steals a weapon that has been carelessly stored could get away with only one year if he commits a crime with it. Usually a person does not steal a weapon if he does not plan to commit a crime. Where is the sense of justice with this kind of distortion? With all deference to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), we are dealing here with an exchange package between Bill C-83 and Bill C-84, this package that was mailed to our offices. The government has openly said that we are dealing with an exchange between capital punishment and peace and security.
Under Bill C-84 the maximum penalty is 25 years, which means a convict can vegetate. At the same time a rapist could get a maximum of 20 years. Why should anyone who has just committed the crime of rape, and who is liable for a maximum of 20 years, run the risk of leaving a witness lying around, for an extra five years?

speechtext:
Eligibility for parole is another controversial aspect in this legislation. My lawyer friend over on the other side has been getting people off on parole. The legislation also focuses on minimum penalties rather than maximum penalties. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has already introduced a bill providing for a maximum penalty of five years for crimes involving use of weapons or firearms, and this seems to me the approach that we should take. But the government has consistently been moving toward minimum sentences or as short sentences as possible in this legislation instead of maximum sentences. It seems to me that we should increase the minimum penalties and lower the maximum penalties, thus eliminating the vegetation that could occur when people are in prison for a long time, yet still retaining sufficient deterrent to fit the crime.
One final point-

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-PROPOSED RESUMPTION OF NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN AIR CANADA AND FINANCE BRANCH EMPLOYEES AT WINNIPEG
LABOUR CONDITIONS-PROPOSED RESUMPTION OF NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN AIR CANADA AND FINANCE BRANCH EMPLOYEES AT WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to outline briefly the problems facing the Air Canada finance branch employees in Winnipeg, there is still a constant fear on the part of employees that Air Canada plans on transferring all the operations of the finance work to other groups of employees, or to contract out such work. The latter was already implemented, several weeks ago, with portions of the finance work historically performed by the Winnipeg employees being contracted out to C.A.E.
I will continue to protest this action taken by Air Canada in the strongest possible terms. There is no doubt in my mind that Air Canada has been taking steps over the last few years to wind up the finance branch in Winnipeg and move the whole operation to Montreal. It is my firm belief that Air Canada is introducing or has already introduced a decentralization program to remove the finance work from Winnipeg. The Liberals have moved enough government departments into the province of Quebec and it is time this was brought to a stop.
This problem in respect of the Air Canada finance branch has been in existence for the last two parliaments. I have been up on my feet about 30 times on this issue, and other opposition spokesmen have been up countless times. Just to give you an indication of what happened, way back on December 12, 1974, this is what the Liberal minister stated, as reported in the Winnipeg Free-Press of that date:
Labour Minister John Munro agreed Wednesday to instruct his department to provide whatever assistance was necessary to try to resolve the differences between the government owned airline Air Canada and its finance department employees.
The difficulties that have flared up anew between the management of Air Canada and its finance branch, located in Winnipeg, were aired in the Commons Wednesday. Opposition members outside the house pointed out that when the finance branch stops operating financial operations of the huge airline grind to a halt.
That was a year and a half ago and we are still going through the same operation all over again. When is this problem going to be resolved? The number of employees involved in Winnipeg is 700. If Air Canada is successful in making the move to Montreal this will be a tremendous loss to Manitoba, and it will certainly disrupt the lives of 700 families.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-SKY SHOPS INVESTIGATION-ROLE OF OFFICIALS OF DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT IN GRANTING LEASE
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-SKY SHOPS INVESTIGATION-ROLE OF OFFICIALS OF DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT IN GRANTING LEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week as reported at page 12609 of Hansard, in attempting to elicit more information concerning the background of the extension of the Sky Shops lease I asked a former minister of transport, now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), to indicate briefly what role members of his senior staff played in this matter, whether these roles were carried out with his knowledge and authorization, and what action, if any, he had taken to ensure that the RCMP had access to all relevant information with regard to these activities.
The minister indicated that he was informed informally concerning an exchange of correspondence between the executive assistant to the then minister of regional economic expansion and his own executive assistant. If I understood him correctly, he also indicated that he really did not have much knowledge of what disposition was made by the RCMP of the correspondence to which he gave them access.
The whole question of how the government deals with the awarding of leases and concessions is obviously of great concern. There is no reason why Sky Shops should be regarded as a unique, or even a rare example. Let us consider, for example, all this company did or had done for it in the period 1970 to 1972. This is a most curious affair. One should remember that while the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was in the transport portfolio, Sky Shops was very active in lobbying.
In the winter of 1970 its campaign began. It deliberately sought to have its lease extended upon terms which dispensed with competitive tenders, something which by definition was, and I believe still is, against stated government policy. Departmental officials in the Department of Transport were contacted. The principal secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), Mr. Lalonde, as he then was, was approached by Mr. Lapointe, who was a chief executive officer of Sky Shops and who had been allotted $10,000 to advance the interests of this company.
A former minister of transport, the Hon. Lionel Chevri-er, was retained to press the company cause, and we have now learned that executive assistants may have been corresponding without the approval, or perhaps even the
Adjournment Debate
knowledge, of their respective ministers with regard to a Sky Shops lease extension.
So I hope this evening-and I appreciate very much his coming here-that the minister can further explain the increasingly complex background of this matter. Perhaps the minister can say how these events, and the correspondence in particular, happened without his knowledge. I am not disputing that he did not know anything about it, but I should like to know more details in retrospect about how this could have occurred. It is not as if others in Ottawa or his own department were not aware of the pressure to change his department's policy on tendering. Is it not logical or likely that at some point in time the minister must have signed some documents recommending to his colleagues on the Treasury Board that the Sky Shops lease be extended on its terms?
For approximately two years personnel in the Department of Transport were lobbied extensively. Can we not assume, as logical members of parliament, that the minister of transport as he then was must have become very curious about the RCMP's interest in his files as they related to Sky Shops? Tonight I hope the minister can shed a little more light on the background of the correspondence and why, in the normal course of events, an ex assistant from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion would be concerned about an airport duty free store lease and why the minister was not informed.
Over five months ago, on November 3, 1975, I asked the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to stay the renewal of the Sky Shops lease, which was not to take effect until the following month, until he was fully satisfied that the renewal was properly obtained. This was not done. Also on the same day I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in concert with his colleague in Transport to investigate thoroughly the circumstances of the Sky Shops leases at both Mirabel and Dorval. To this point in time we still have no assurance that parliament has all the answers to why the leases were renewed and granted on the terms which prevailed.
Therefore I ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the former minister of the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion and Transport, to join with me and support the calling of a judicial inquiry into the entire background of the Sky Shops lease extension, and tendering procedures at Mirabel for concessions there. Until such time as our committee procedures are modified so that more effective investigation can be done there, a judicial inquiry is the only way to learn what has to be done to improve the ways in which tendering procedures, or the lack of them, are administered in cases such as this.

Mr. Speaker, I was advised late this afternoon of the intentions of the hon. member, but of course I had no way to know until three or four moments ago what kind of a statement he wished to make this evening. He has made a number of comments. I am not in a position to test the veracity of them. They involve various people who were engaged in the matter, and things of that sort. I am sure he would not expect me in the three minutes I have to try to deal with them, or indeed either to accept or refute them. I repeat that I have heard some of the comments only in the last few moments.

April 12, 1976
Adjournment Debate
The late show tonight is based on the questions the hon. member asked me on Thursday. It is to those that I am prepared to address myself. Specifically he asked in the first instance, I think, about the reason I was not curious as to why the RCMP would have asked me in the first place if I would object to any search of my correspondence or a look at my files from my Transport days. The answer is that when they came to see me they told me it was in connection with the Sky Shops affair. I said, "Fine", and I gave them the authorization. I am sure the hon. gentleman will agree it was entirely appropriate for me to do so. I do not know from any questioning or inquiries what the resolution of that might be. That is the situation which exists at this moment. I have not since that time been questioned or checked by the RCMP or by anyone else. Nor have I sought any sort of information as to what the results were.
The hon. member knows very well of course how I learned informally of the existence of certain correspondence between my executive assistant and the executive assistant to the then the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. I do not think he will object to my saying he was among those who advised me of its existence. It was only in that way that I became aware of it; that is, by statements by him and other people who I assume in the very nature of things found out this was the case. I do not know specifically what the contents of those letters or correspondence were. I have not seen them.
On the final point having to do with-I am trying to paraphrase the hon. member's question-whether or not I would have been advised of this kind of correspondence, I think he must be aware that in the normal course there are many occasions on which members of cabinet, officials, and various others, including I might say members of this House, write letters of inquiry on behalf of various people. I regard all this as being entirely legitimate and appropriate, but I think that anyone who suggests that a minister or, for that matter, a member of parliament is aware of every piece of correspondence seeking information is being unreasonable.
In all fairness, a great many such inquiries are made, but to the best of my knowledge and recollection there was never any awareness on my part that any such inquiry was made. Also, until such time as I see the correspondence, or it is made public, it would be unfair to suggest that any member of my staff, or anyone else, would engage in any impropriety, or anything like it.
I realize again that once one of these issues is raised it creates real problems in terms of obtaining rational and reasonable views. In this case I am aware that the gentleman in question has suffered unfairly moments of anxiety as a result of this. My only comment is that I hope the matter is cleared up as quickly as possible. I can only repeat what I said in the beginning, and answer as I did on Thursday; that is the full extent of my awareness of the matter which the hon. member has raised.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CANADIAN POSITION ON INVOLVEMENT OF CUBA IN AFRICA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CANADIAN POSITION ON INVOLVEMENT OF CUBA IN AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 23 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) certain questions about his Cuba visit. I asked specifically if he had registered any further protest about Cuban involvement in military operations in Africa. In my question, as reported at page 12051 of Hansard, I attributed to the Prime Minister the statement that "Premier Fidele Castro was sending troops to Africa with a great deal of thought and feeling." I went on to say that I would be interested in any new information concerning the Cuban involvement and, if such information was available, in knowing the current position of the administration with respect to this unhappy situation. The Prime Minister was in a real flap. He answered;
I must point out that the hon. member has grossly and inaccurately misquoted me.
I then said:
If I am grossly and inaccurately misquoting the Prime Minister so did the Globe and Mail this morning.
I then followed my remark with a supplementary question. I wanted to know if there had been any official protest concerning this war involvement on the part of Cuba and, if so, what was the form of the protest. The Prime Minister answered as follows:
I am informed that the misquote in the Globe and Mail was a quote from some American paper, so the hon. member is twice removed from the truth by two very big barriers.
He went on to say that, oh, yes, he had protested. Another minister had protested the involvement. He ended by saying, "We are opposed to that kind of intervention".
I suggest that the government adheres to a double standard. Today the Prime Minister, supported by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), had no hesitation in refusing financial assistance to a certain athletic event which is to take place in Canada, because it is understood that South Africans may attend that event and the government takes exception to the present status of segregation within that country. I do not disagree with that position; I simply ask why, if you do not agree with the internal activities of another country, do you involve yourself with Cuba? Why is there this double standard ? Why is there this involvement in the case of Cuba but not in the case of South Africa?
A few months ago the Prime Minister shunned a ploughing match near my riding in Ontario. His stated reason for shunning it was that two old Rhodesians happened to turn up and proposed to participate. He said that in no way would he give that ploughing match his blessing by appearing at the function.
The Prime Minister claims I misquoted him on March 23. Well, the remark I attributed to him, to which he referred, was carried in the New York Times. The New York Times reported the Prime Minister as saying that:
... Fidel Castro is a man of world statute, one 'very well informed about Africa,' who sent 10,000 Cuban soldiers to fight in Angola's civil war only after 'a great deal of thought and feeling for the situation.'

I notice it has the blessing of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). I can well under-

stand the Prime Minister having a lot in common with that hon. member, knowing their backgrounds. Not only did the New York Times attribute that quote, but the Prime Minister stated in this House in answer to a question from the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I quote:
In so far as Premier Castro's views, he made them known to me. I have the feeling that he has a good knowledge of Africa and a good feeling for the realities there.
Right in this House he said virtually the same thing I attributed to him in the question to which he has since taken such exception.
Some time ago I pointed out to the House, in the form of a question to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), that we were giving extensive aid to Cuba through CIDA and the Export Development Corporation. Something over $100 million has been extended. The point that the President of the Privy Council and the Prime Minister have managed to sidestep is that Canada has no obligation to assist a country that is capable of sending troops, take your pick, anywhere from 6,000 to 12,000 according to reports, to fight in civil wars thousands of miles from its shores. Not only have they chosen to go into Angola, but the troops are now remaining in Angola and are active in seven other African countries which presumably have aggressive desires within the continent of Africa. Not only is this so, but when the government suggests it does not want to allow internal considerations in these countries to change its aid programs, it is contradicting itself.
About two years ago when the President of the Privy Council was Secretary of State for External Affairs he had no hesitation in cutting off government aid to India because the government felt that country had gone against Canada's wishes and detonated a nuclear device built with plutonium from a Canadian nuclear reactor. I am not disagreeing with this position, but what I find most remarkable is that the Prime Minister has embarrassed us with many of our allies around the world, including Venezuela. If I had more time I would read the quotes coming out of Caracas concerning the visit of the Prime Minister to Cuba.
The Prime Minister has embarrassed us as far as our world position is concerned, stating that he has a kind of token opposition to the Cuban involvement in Africa, but judging from his reply of March 23, in no way is he prepared to state to this House what official protests he has made.
Has he indicated we will withdraw our economic assistance to that country if it does not cease and desist from its
Adjournment Debate
aggressive tendencies, not only by sending troops to Africa but also making a contribution to South American countries, one at least bordering Venezuela from where we import a very large amount of our oil? The House deserves a better explanation than what it has had up to the present time.

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CANADIAN POSITION ON INVOLVEMENT OF CUBA IN AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course Canada's foreign affairs policy is not and could not be based on news reports in the Globe and Mail and the New York Times which seem to be the sources of information on the subject on which the hon. member opposite just spoke. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated the opposite very clearly in this House on March 23. He concluded his statement by reaffirming without any ambiguity, and I quote:
We are opposed to that kind of intervention.
The hon. member gave a strange example of stopping aid to India after the nuclear explosion in May 1974, and the case of apartheid in South Africa. These are two cases where international bodies-in one case the International Atomic Energy through the NPT and other multilateral agreements, and in the other case the General Assembly of the United Nations-have adopted clear resolutions voted upon by the world, to which of course we adhere. Consequently we took the course of action which is the wish and the will of the Canadian people represented by the Prime Minister and the various actions taken by our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen).
The case of the conduct of Cuba and its involvement in Angola has been repeatedly exposed to the House and to the public through the statement made in the United Nations General Assembly last fall by our Canadian representative in the Fourth Committee. It was then later repeated in the minister's release dated January 20, 1976, and again in his press statement of February 18 when he announced Canada's recognition of the People's Republic of Angola. He reaffirmed our opposition to the continued presence of foreign troops.
With regard to an official protest to Cuba, the Prime Minister, as the hon. member is aware, has spoken directly to Premier Castro on this subject. This is repeated each time a Canadian minister has occasion to meet his Cuban counterpart and to my knowledge the most recent instance was the meeting between our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and his Cuban counterpart. I think this is a very clear case in which the Prime Minister of Canada is representing the wishes of Canadians, as usual, Mr. Speaker.
